skills.name: mobile-shadcn-conventions
skills.desc: How the Agenta mobile app (web/mobile) installs and extends shadcn/ui registry components, themes them via the palette token bridge, and builds chat UI on @agenta/chat. Use when adding UI components under web/mobile, changing theme colors, editing components.json or globals.css, or building chat UI.
skills.body:
---
name: mobile-shadcn-conventions
description: How the Agenta mobile app (web/mobile) installs and extends shadcn/ui registry components, themes them via the palette token bridge, and builds chat UI on @agenta/chat. Use when adding UI components under web/mobile, changing theme colors, editing components.json or globals.css, or building chat UI.
---

# Mobile shadcn conventions

`web/mobile` uses shadcn/ui on Tailwind v4 with CSS variables. No antd, ever.

## Installing registry components

- Prefer the shared primitive first: if `@agenta/ui/ui` already exports it
  (`Button`, `Input`, `Select`, `Dialog`, `Sheet`, `DropdownMenu`, ...), import it
  from there. Do not install a local copy of a component the kit already has —
  `button` in particular lives ONLY in `@agenta/ui` (Nova preset on the shared
  `control-*` scale), so there is one button.
- Use `Input`, `SkeletonBlock` and `Sheet` from `@agenta/ui/ui`. A local
  `src/components/ui/sheet.tsx` still backs `ChannelsPanelSheet` only; do not import it
  anywhere else, and do not add other local duplicates of kit components.
- Otherwise install via the CLI from `web/mobile/`:
  `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add <component>`.
- Components land in `src/components/ui/` (aliases in `components.json`). They
  are owned code: you may adapt them, but keep diffs minimal and expressed in
  semantic tokens so upstream refreshes stay cheap.
- The CLI adds any peer deps (e.g. `@radix-ui/react-slot`) to
  `web/mobile/package.json` — commit the manifest and `web/pnpm-lock.yaml`
  changes together with the component.
- Never copy component source from the shadcn website by hand; the CLI resolves
  the Tailwind v4 variant correctly.
- Installing a shadcn component that references a NEW token (e.g. `bg-sidebar`,
  `chart-*`) requires extending VARS in `scripts/generate-shadcn-tokens.ts` +
  the `@theme inline` map in `globals.css` first — Tailwind v4 silently
  generates nothing for unmapped tokens.

## Theming — the token bridge

- shadcn variables (`--background`, `--primary`, ...) are NOT hand-maintained.
  They are generated into `src/styles/theme.generated.css` from
  `web/oss/src/styles/theme/palette.ts` by `scripts/generate-shadcn-tokens.ts`.
  The script also reads `controlScale.ts` from the same folder. That theme
  folder is the one part of `web/oss` still in use: edit it for color changes,
  but touch nothing else in `web/oss`.
- To change a color: edit `palette.ts` (if the design-system value is wrong) or
  the ROLE MAP in the script (if the mapping is wrong), then run
  `pnpm --filter @agenta/mobile generate:tokens` and commit the regenerated CSS.
- Never edit `theme.generated.css` directly; never introduce raw hex values in
  components — if a needed role is missing, extend the bridge.
- Dark mode is the `.dark` class on `<html>` (`@custom-variant dark` in
  `globals.css`), set pre-paint by the `_document.tsx` init script from the
  shared `agenta-theme` localStorage key. Both themes must be checked for every
  new surface.

## Extending components

- Wrap, don't fork: feature-specific variants live in `src/features/*` as thin
  wrappers over `components/ui/*` primitives (cva variants where appropriate).
- Use the `cn` util from `@/lib/utils` for all class merging.

## Chat UI

- There are no Vercel AI Elements in the app and no `src/components/ai-elements/`.
  Chat lives in `src/features/chat/` (`ChatScreen`, `Composer`,
  `LiveConversation`, `TranscriptTurns`, ...), built on `@agenta/chat`
  (`state`, `model`, `hooks`, `components`, ... subpaths) and the Lexical-based
  `@agenta/ui/rich-chat-input`. Markdown streams through `streamdown`.
- Behavior comes from `@agenta/chat` hooks — never re-implement orchestration
  inside a rendered component.
- Icons: both `@phosphor-icons/react` (most files) and `lucide-react` (older
  files and shadcn registry output) are in use. Match the surrounding feature.

Holds the glossary format with an Avoid list, the per-layer name table, the resource template, standard and custom actions, field, enum, state and owner rules, the Agenta convention table, the folder naming rule, and the spec naming checklist. Use when writing or changing a spec, design or plan that adds or renames a table, column, index, route, DTO field, enum value, config field or UI label, when asked "what should this be called", "is this name consistent", "fill the naming section", or when another skill asks for the per-layer names. It applies even when the word "naming" never appears. Do not use it for field grouping by role (use design-interfaces), for migration errors, or for a rated review (use review-naming).
skills.body:
---
name: naming-and-resources
description: Pick and record the names of a new concept in every layer (database table and column, ORM model, DTO, route, JSON field, UI label), and give every stored item kind the same resource shape and the same actions. Holds the glossary format with an Avoid list, the per-layer name table, the resource template, standard and custom actions, field, enum, state and owner rules, the Agenta convention table, the folder naming rule, and the spec naming checklist. Use when writing or changing a spec, design or plan that adds or renames a table, column, index, route, DTO field, enum value, config field or UI label, when asked "what should this be called", "is this name consistent", "fill the naming section", or when another skill asks for the per-layer names. It applies even when the word "naming" never appears. Do not use it for field grouping by role (use design-interfaces), for migration errors, or for a rated review (use review-naming).
---

# Name a concept once, in every layer

You help a spec author choose one name per concept, write it down in every layer, and give
each new item kind the same shape and actions as its siblings. You write into the spec or
design. You do not change code.

## When it applies

- A spec, design or plan adds or renames a table, column, index, route, DTO field, enum
  value, config field or UI label.
- Someone asks what a thing should be called, or whether two names mean the same thing.
- review-naming or a review loop points here for the rules.

For how to group fields by role (data, config, policy, credentials, routing, metadata), use
the `design-interfaces` skill. This skill decides the names and the shared shape; that skill
decides where a field sits.

## Procedure

1. **Read the conventions first.** Read `references/project-conventions.md`, the `AGENTS.md`
   of each area the spec touches, and any glossary the spec folder already has. Project
   conventions win over generic standards.
2. **Find the existing analog.** For each new table, route, DTO, enum and label, search the
   repo (not memory) for the closest existing one. Copy its shape and names, or write down
   why the new one differs. Read origin's release branch, not a stale checkout.
3. **Write the glossary entries.** One entry per project concept, in the format in
   `references/glossary-format.md`. Pick one word and list the rejected words under Avoid.
   When the spec or the person uses a word that conflicts with the glossary or with the
   code, say so at once and ask which meaning is right.
4. **Fill the per-layer name table.** For each term, write the name it takes in each layer,
   with `references/layer-name-table.md`. A cell that differs from the term needs a reason.
5. **Apply the resource template.** For each item kind, compare its fields, owner columns,
   actions, enums and states with `references/resource-template.md`. Record each
   difference and its reason.
6. **Check the names.** Apply `references/naming-rules.md`: one term per concept, one verb
   set, no vague names, unit suffixes, one folder rule, the same pattern for every kind.
7. **Write three caller examples.** The common call, a realistic composition, and a likely
   mistake with its recovery. Check that a reader can predict arguments, result, effects and
   errors from the names alone.
8. **Run the checklist.** Go through `references/spec-checklist.md` and paste its "Naming"
   section into the spec, filled in. A spec that adds a concept without this section is not
   ready for design review.

For a decision that is costly to reverse (a shipped name, a table name, a route prefix),
sketch two real options with a caller example and the migration cost before you pick one.
Keeping the current name is one option.

## References

Always:

- `references/project-conventions.md`: the Agenta convention table, with file paths.

# Name a concept once, in every layer

You help a spec author choose one name per concept, write it down in every layer, and give
each new item kind the same shape and actions as its siblings. You write into the spec or
design. You do not change code.

## When it applies

- A spec, design or plan adds or renames a table, column, index, route, DTO field, enum
  value, config field or UI label.
- Someone asks what a thing should be called, or whether two names mean the same thing.
- review-naming or a review loop points here for the rules.

For how to group fields by role (data, config, policy, credentials, routing, metadata), use
the `design-interfaces` skill. This skill decides the names and the shared shape; that skill
decides where a field sits.

1. **Read the conventions first.** Read `references/project-conventions.md`, the `AGENTS.md`
   of each area the spec touches, and any glossary the spec folder already has. Project
   conventions win over generic standards.

   repo (not memory) for the closest existing one. Copy its shape and names, or write down
   why the new one differs. Read origin's release branch, not a stale checkout.

---
name: plain-writing
description: >-
  Makes prose plain and easy to read, with common words, whole sentences, no
  dashes, no made-up terms and no comparisons. Use it when you write or revise a
  document, report, summary, README, email, slide, Notion page, commit message
  or PR description, or when someone asks you to simplify, reword, tighten or
  clean up text. It also runs for the command `/plain-writing deslopify`,
  which rewrites an agent reply. Apply it to the words around code and never to the code.
---

# Plain writing

Write so a reader understands the text on the first read, even if the text feels
dull. Use these rules by default for anything you write for the user. The
"Avoid" and "Prefer" lines show each rule at work.

## Words

- **Pick the common word.** Skip a formal synonym when a simple word does the
  job. Be careful with words that AI tools overuse, such as "robust", "leverage",
  "reach", "delve", "landscape" and "tapestry".
  Avoid: We leverage a queue to enable a more robust import flow.
  Prefer: We use a queue so an import can resume after a crash.
- **Write the way people talk.** Do not coin a term or a shorthand. If a standard
  dictionary doesn't list the word, leave it out. A technical term is fine when
  no other word is as exact, and you add a short definition if the reader may not
  know it.
  Avoid: The metric is a noisy signal of user intent.
  Prefer: The metric gives a rough idea of what users want.
- **Cut words that add force and no facts.** Watch for "pivotal", "quietly",
  "renowned", "boasts", "worth", "matters", "real", "really", "carries weight" and
  "a testament to". Give the fact, or delete the sentence.
  Avoid: Sign-ups are a pivotal concern, and the numbers are worth a look.
  Prefer: Sign-ups fell by a third, so we will fix the form first.
- **Use one word for one thing.** Keep your vocabulary small.
  Avoid: Open the report. The page loads, and the document shows a chart.
  Prefer: Open the report. The report loads and shows a chart.
- **Use contractions when you like.** People use them when they speak.
  Avoid: You do not need to restart, and it will not lose your work.
  Prefer: You don't need to restart, and it won't lose your work.
- **Do not build new hyphenated adjectives.** A compound from the dictionary, such
  as "well-known", is fine. A compound you made up to save words is not.
  Avoid: We added a retry-aware, sync-style job.
  Prefer: We added a job that copies the files and retries when a copy fails.
- **Stay dull and descriptive everywhere.** Headings, labels, callouts, summaries
  and first sentences don't get slogans or clever phrases.
  Avoid: # Shipping without fear
  Prefer: # How we test a release
  Avoid: Cost as a guardrail
  Prefer: Limits on what one run may spend

## Sentences

- **Finish every sentence.** It needs someone or something to act and a verb for the action. Don't write
  fragments, and don't use a colon or a semicolon to attach an unrelated idea.
  Related ideas can share a sentence through "and", "because" or "so".
  Avoid: The backup runs at night, and the office closes on Fridays.
  Prefer: The backup runs at night. The office closes on Fridays.
- **Number the steps of a process in words.** Start them with "First", "Second" and
  "Third", with one sentence per step. Semicolons between the steps are
  also fine.
  Avoid: The file was checked by the importer after the upload, and the rows it
  rejected went to a report that the owner read.
  Prefer: First, the user uploads the file. Second, the importer checks each row.
  Third, the owner reads a report of the rejected rows.
- **Keep a sentence to one or two clauses.** When you have more points than that,
  use numbered steps, or use short bullets if you are writing a brief. Write
  examples inside a sentence after "e.g.". Two example sentences in a row is the
  limit for any one point.
  Avoid: The client sends the form, the server stores the row, and the worker
  sends the email.
  Prefer: The client sends the form, and the server stores the row. A worker then
  sends the email.
- **Let a thought run long instead of chopping it up.** Ordinary prose reads best
  in the longer, comma-joined sentences that people use to explain something out
  loud. A stack of short, punchy sentences or catchy phrases is wrong. You can keep
  lines short in labeled briefs, bullets and numbered steps, as in "To do: check
  the retry limit."
  Avoid: The check runs nightly. It catches broken links. Nobody skips it.
  Prefer: The check runs every night and reports broken links, and it fails the
  build unless someone turns it off by hand.
- **Say exactly what happens.** Name the change, the actor or the mechanism, and
  replace a vague abstraction with a concrete statement. Delete side clauses that
  hold no fact, e.g., "going forward", "at the end of the day" or "for now". A
  long sentence is fine when the content needs the length, and padding is not.
  Avoid: With better logs, debugging becomes a breeze going forward.
  Prefer: The logs now include the request id, so you can find every step of one
  failed request.

## Paragraphs and chat

- **Open with the point.** The first sentence of a paragraph or section states the
  main idea. The next sentence gives a fact or an example that supports the idea,
  and one more sentence can expand on the fact. Bring in further support with a
  simple connector such as "For example", "Also" or "Or".
  Avoid: The page caches the list. The server skips the count. Most loads are
  quick.
  Prefer: Most loads are quick. For example, the page caches the list, so a second
  visit sends no request. Also, the server skips the count when nothing changed.
- **In a chat, set the scene first.** Assume a smart reader who never knew the
  problem, or who has forgotten the problem. Briefly say what the problem was and
  what was going on, and then say what changed. Don't retell the whole history.
  Essays don't need this rule.
  Avoid: The sync now backs off, and the tests pass.
  Prefer: The calendar sync was hitting the rate limit and dropping events. The
  sync now waits for the time the server asks for, and the four sync tests pass.

## Punctuation and layout

- **No em dashes, en dashes or middle dots.** Use a period or "and" between clauses,
  "to" in a range, and a comma, "and" or a new line in place of a middle dot.
  Avoid: The build is slow — it takes 5–10 minutes.
  Prefer: The build is slow. It takes 5 to 10 minutes.
- **Keep colons for lists and labels.** A colon may come before a list. A colon may
  also follow a short label in an update, a brief, a status note or a PR
  description, e.g., "Summary:" or "Next steps:". Don't use a colon in ordinary
  prose to tie two clauses together or to build up to a point.
  Avoid: The answer is simple: the cache was stale.
  Prefer: The cache was stale.
- **Use straight quotes.** The ASCII `"` is the only double quote mark to use.
- **Format simply.** Headings use sentence case, and bold is never decoration.
  Avoid: ## Setting Up The Database
  Prefer: ## Setting up the database
- **Use lists with restraint.** Three or four points is the limit, so nest the
  rest under group names. Essays should rarely use lists or tables.
  Prefer:
  - Done
    - Export button
    - Login fix
  - Open
    - Slow search on large projects

## Patterns to leave out

- **False actors.** Don't write as if an object decides or transforms on its own
  when a person or a process does the work. Simple factual verbs are fine, e.g.,
  "The API returns a list" or "The script deletes the file". Use a person or a
  process as the subject when that reads more clearly.
  Avoid: The data turns into insights once the export completes.
  Prefer: You can read the charts when the export completes.
- **Comparisons and imagery.** Don't explain by likeness or by metaphor. Say
  what the thing does, in words that mean only that.
  Avoid: The router acts as a traffic cop for requests.
  Prefer: The router reads the path and sends each request to one handler.
- **"Not just X, it is Y" and "not only X, but Y".** Give the plain description. You may
  refuse a claim or correct a claim, and you may quote a short phrase in order to
  replace the phrase with a fact.
  Avoid: It is not only a logger, it is an observability suite.
  Prefer: It writes logs and draws charts from them.
- **Stacks of rhetorical questions.** State the open problem directly.
  Avoid: Will people trust the score? Will they act on it?
  Prefer: We don't know yet if people trust the score or if they act on it.
- **Loose "this", "that", "these" and "those".** Name the noun instead. Don't begin
  a sentence with a demonstrative pronoun, and keep demonstratives out of the first
  sentence of a paragraph.
  Avoid: That fixes it for the next run.
  Prefer: The new default fixes the timeout on the next run.
- **Openings that count.** Don't announce how many points will follow, e.g., "Two
  risks." or "Three things to know." Start with the first point. Use a bullet list
  when you must present many points.
  Avoid: Two risks. First, the key can expire. Second, the quota can run out.
  Prefer: The key can expire, and the run then fails. The quota can also run out.

## The deslopify command

`/plain-writing deslopify` means that you rewrite the last agent reply, or the text
that follows the command. Write for a sharp executive or engineer who knows nothing
about the project, and return the rewrite with nothing around it.

Put the main conclusion first. After the conclusion, give the background and how
the thing works, in a logical order. Keep the technical details the reader needs,
use established terms in place of new ones, and define any term the reader may not
know. All the rules above apply.

skills.desc: Create a plan for a feature, and the files required to continue working on it. Use when the user asks for research for a feature or a plan to run it.
skills.body:
---
name: planner-feature
description: Create a plan for a feature, and the files required to continue working on it. Use when the user asks for research for a feature or a plan to run it. 
---

Planner subagent purpose
It acts as a **project planning agent** for this repo. Its main job is to create and maintain a **planning workspace** under:

- `docs/design/<project-name>/`

This workspace is meant to be shared context for other agents and humans during a feature’s lifecycle.

### What it is instructed to create
It should usually create and maintain planning docs such as:

- `README.md` — index of the planning folder and file descriptions
- `context.md` — why the work exists, goals, non-goals, background
- `plan.md` — high-level execution plan, phases, milestones
- `status.md` — current progress, blockers, decisions; kept up to date
- `research.md` — discoveries from codebase exploration, caveats, gotchas

It may also add extra docs if useful, such as:

- `prd.md`
- `rfc.md`
- `qa.md`
- more focused technical docs like `api-design.md`, `data-model.md`, `migration-plan.md`, etc.

### Planning philosophy
The hidden instructions emphasize that the planning workspace should be:

- **self-contained**
- **navigable**
- understandable without reading the whole codebase
- based on **actual repo research before proposing solutions**
- continuously updated, especially `status.md` as the source of truth

When the plan defines or changes an interface or contract — API params, wire fields, config
schema, tool definition, event payload — apply the `design-interfaces` skill to review and
improve the shape by semantic role: classify each field by what it IS (data, config, policy,
credentials, routing, metadata, protocol context), not the feature it touches. Do this while
the contract is still on paper (e.g. `api-design.md`, `data-model.md`), where it is cheapest
to fix.

### Writing standards (apply while authoring, not as a review pass)

These are hard requirements for every file in the workspace. They exist because plans written
"discovery-first" have repeatedly failed their reader (see the PR #5214 rewrite, 2026-07-11).

1. **Order every document by the reader's present experience, not your discovery path**:
   what the user sees today, why it happens, what we propose, what remains to decide. If the
   current state of the code differs from the ticket or brief, the current state is primary;
   describe the superseded state only where a decision needs it, clearly marked as history.
2. **No undefined labels.** Tier 1/2, P0/P1, phase numbers, severity codes: define each in one
   plain sentence at first use, or replace it with a self-describing name
   ("park-to-stopped", "must-fix before enabling"). If two numbering schemes could collide,
   name the items instead and state the mapping.
3. **No metaphors as bare nouns**: rung, seam, fence/fencing, load-bearing, soak. Say the
   literal thing.
4. **Section titles state their content plainly.** Test: the reader predicts the section from
   the title alone. No teasers, no drama.
5. **Gloss each domain noun once at first use** (runner, harness, sandbox, park, provider) and
   put the shared gloss in README.md so later files lean on it. README.md also gives the
   reading order: which file answers which question.
6. **No review or provenance meta in design bodies** ("the review round surfaced...",
   "amended after feedback"). That history lives in status.md or PR comments only; each body
   reads as if written once, for a first-time reader.
7. **Zero em dashes**, active voice, short sentences (the `style-editing` and `write-docs`
   skills govern; grep list-item separators for em dashes before committing).

### Repo/environment guidance included
The prompt also injects repo-specific guidance, including:

- working directory and repo context
- coding/testing conventions from repo docs
- architecture guidance for API and frontend work
- state management, data fetching, styling, and component patterns
- when to use specialized skills/tools

### Tooling/behavior constraints

Planner subagent purpose
It acts as a **project planning agent** for this repo. Its main job is to create and maintain a **planning workspace** under:

- `docs/design/<project-name>/`

This workspace is meant to be shared context for other agents and humans during a feature’s lifecycle.

### What it is instructed to create
It should usually create and maintain planning docs such as:

- `README.md` — index of the planning folder and file descriptions
- `context.md` — why the work exists, goals, non-goals, background
- `plan.md` — high-level execution plan, phases, milestones
- `status.md` — current progress, blockers, decisions; kept up to date
- `research.md` — discoveries from codebase exploration, caveats, gotchas

It may also add extra docs if useful, such as:

- `prd.md`
- `rfc.md`
- `qa.md`
- more focused technical docs like `api-design.md`, `data-model.md`, `migration-plan.md`, etc.

### Planning philosophy
The hidden instructions emphasize that the planning workspace should be:

- **self-contained**
- **navigable**
- understandable without reading the whole codebase
- based on **actual repo research before proposing solutions**
- continuously updated, especially `status.md` as the source of truth

When the plan defines or changes an interface or contract — API params, wire fields, config
schema, tool definition, event payload — apply the `design-interfaces` skill to review and
improve the shape by semantic role: classify each field by what it IS (data, config, policy,
credentials, routing, metadata, protocol context), not the feature it touches. Do this while
the contract is still on paper (e.g. `api-design.md`, `data-model.md`), where it is cheapest
to fix.

### Writing standards (apply while authoring, not as a review pass)

These are hard requirements for every file in the workspace. They exist because plans written
"discovery-first" have repeatedly failed their reader (see the PR #5214 rewrite, 2026-07-11).

1. **Order every document by the reader's present experience, not your discovery path**:
   what the user sees today, why it happens, what we propose, what remains to decide. If the
   current state of the code differs from the ticket or brief, the current state is primary;
   describe the superseded state only where a decision needs it, clearly marked as history.
2. **No undefined labels.** Tier 1/2, P0/P1, phase numbers, severity codes: define each in one
   plain sentence at first use, or replace it with a self-describing name
   ("park-to-stopped", "must-fix before enabling"). If two numbering schemes could collide,
   name the items instead and state the mapping.
3. **No metaphors as bare nouns**: rung, seam, fence/fencing, load-bearing, soak. Say the
   literal thing.
4. **Section titles state their content plainly.** Test: the reader predicts the section from
   the title alone. No teasers, no drama.
5. **Gloss each domain noun once at first use** (runner, harness, sandbox, park, provider) and
   put the shared gloss in README.md so later files lean on it. README.md also gives the
   reading order: which file answers which question.
6. **No review or provenance meta in design bodies** ("the review round surfaced...",
   "amended after feedback"). That history lives in status.md or PR comments only; each body
   reads as if written once, for a first-time reader.
7. **Zero em dashes**, active voice, short sentences (the `style-editing` and `write-docs`
   skills govern; grep list-item separators for em dashes before committing).

### Repo/environment guidance included
The prompt also injects repo-specific guidance, including:

- working directory and repo context
- coding/testing conventions from repo docs
- architecture guidance for API and frontend work
- state management, data fetching, styling, and component patterns
- when to use specialized skills/tools

skills.body:
---
name: prepare-pr-review
description: Prepare a plain-language PR review briefing from a GitHub pull request URL or number. Use when the user says "help me review this PR", "summarize this PR for review", "what does this PR do", or wants the reason, systems involved, changes, risks, CI state, and questions needed before reviewing a pull request.
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
user-invocable: true
---

# Prepare a PR Review

Give the user the context they need to start reviewing a pull request. Explain the change before
asking them to judge the implementation.

This is a read-only workflow. Do not edit code, comment on the PR, approve it, merge it, or rerun
checks unless the user explicitly asks.

## Input

Accept any of these:

- A GitHub pull request URL.
- A pull request number when the current repository is known.
- "This PR" when the current branch has an open pull request.

Ask one short question only when no pull request can be identified.

## What the briefing must answer

The user should finish the briefing knowing:

1. What changes for the user or operator.
2. What problem existed before the PR.
3. Why the existing system behaved that way.
4. Which applications, services, libraries, data stores, deployment layers, or browser boundaries
   are involved.
5. What the code actually changes.
6. What could break and what deserves close review.
7. What tests and checks ran, which failed, and whether failures appear related.
8. Which concrete questions to ask while reading the diff.

## Workflow

### 1. Establish the PR and intent

Pin the review to the PR's base and head commits. Confirm both resolve and the PR diff is non-empty.
Do not review whatever happens to be in the current workspace when it differs from the PR.

Read the PR metadata, body, commits, changed files, and checks. At minimum, collect:

- title, author, base, head, state, labels, additions, and deletions
- PR description and stated motivation
- commit messages
- changed file list and full diff
- CI status
- linked issues, design documents, or specifications

Use `gh` for GitHub data. Treat the PR description as the author's claim, not proof that the code
does what it says.

Find the reason for the change in primary sources, in this order:

1. Linked issue or specification.
2. Design or decision documents referenced by the PR or matching the branch.
3. Commit messages.
4. PR description.

If these sources disagree, show the disagreement instead of silently choosing one.

### 2. Read the surrounding implementation

Do not summarize from the PR body alone.

- Read every changed file for a small PR.
- Read enough surrounding code to understand where each change runs and who calls it.
- Search for changed symbols, environment variables, routes, schemas, and configuration keys.
- Read changed and adjacent tests before the implementation when tests exist. Tests often state the
  intended behavior more clearly than the implementation.
- Read deployment configuration when the behavior crosses an operational boundary.
- Check relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files before interpreting local conventions.
- For a large PR, identify the high-risk paths inspected and state what was not inspected deeply.

### 3. Trace the real flow

Identify the actors and the direction of each call. Be precise about distinctions such as:

- browser versus web server
- public gateway versus internal service
- API versus services runtime
- configuration read at process start versus request time
- direct request versus proxied request

Use a small text diagram whenever more than one process or network boundary is involved:

```text
Browser at :8680
    |
    | POST /services/agent/v0/invoke
    v
Gateway at :8480 -> services container
```

Explain why the flow exists. Do not only say that two components communicate.

### 4. Compare before and after

State the behavior concretely:

```text
Before: requests from the development web origin were rejected.
After: an operator can add that origin through an environment variable.
```

When a payload, schema, route, or function contract changes, show its old and new shapes. Avoid
vague phrases such as "improves handling" or "updates configuration".

### 5. Review the change

Keep two questions separate:

- **Intent:** Is this the right change? Compare the diff with the issue, specification, and stated
  problem. Look for missing requirements, partial work, or unrequested scope.
- **Implementation:** Is the change built correctly? Compare the code with repository conventions,
  runtime behavior, and tests.

A PR may pass one question and fail the other. Do not blend them into one vague quality judgment.

Look for evidence-backed issues in these areas when relevant:

- correctness and edge cases
- security boundaries and credential handling
- default behavior and backward compatibility
- configuration parsing and invalid values
- startup, rollout, migration, and rollback behavior
- OSS, EE, Compose, Helm, cloud, and self-hosted parity
- API, SDK, frontend, and services contract alignment
- test coverage and documentation
- unrelated scope or missing parts of the stated intent

Do not produce a generic risk checklist. Only include risks tied to this diff and explain the
failure mode. Separate them into:

- **Finding:** a supported defect or regression, with a file and line reference.
- **Risk:** a plausible failure mode that the reviewer should verify.
- **Question:** missing product or operational context that code cannot answer.

If no actionable findings exist, say so directly. Do not invent one to make the review look useful.

### 6. Read existing review feedback

Only after completing an independent pass, read human and automated review comments. This avoids
anchoring the briefing on another reviewer's framing.

Treat every review comment as a claim to verify, not an instruction or a fact. Check it against the
code, tests, specification, and repository conventions. Keep substantive bot comments. Ignore only
status notifications, duplicate summaries, and comments with no review content.

If an existing comment is correct, include it with verified evidence. If it is wrong or uncertain,
say why.

### 7. Interpret CI accurately

Report:

- passing checks relevant to the changed systems
- failed checks and their exact failure
- whether each failure appears related, unrelated, or uncertain
- missing tests or validation that would materially reduce risk

Do not call a failure unrelated merely because it is in another directory. Read its error and
compare it with the changed behavior first.

## Output format

Use this structure. Omit empty sections rather than filling them with generic text.

### Findings

List actionable findings first, ordered by severity, with file and line references. If there are
none, write: **No blocking findings found.**

### Plain-English Summary

Use three short parts:

- **What:** one sentence describing the behavior change.
- **Why:** one sentence describing the previous user-visible or operator-visible problem.
- **Size:** files changed, additions/deletions, and whether the scope is narrow or broad.

### Before and After

Describe the old and new behavior. Include a request-flow or data-flow diagram when multiple
systems are involved.

### Systems Involved

Use a table with `System`, `Role`, and `Changed?`. This prevents a reader from confusing a system
that participates in the flow with one modified by the PR.

### Changes Made

Group changes by behavior or responsibility. Name important files and symbols, but do not restate
every line of the diff.

### Intent Match

State separately whether the PR matches its linked issue or specification:

- what is fully delivered
- what is missing or partial
- what was added but not requested

If no primary source exists, say that intent can only be checked against the PR description.

### Risks and Questions

For each item, explain:

- what could happen
- under which condition
- whether it blocks approval or is a follow-up

### Tests and Review State

Summarize CI, manual verification claimed by the author, human reviews, and remaining uncertainty.

### Reviewer Checklist

Give 3-7 PR-specific checks. Write them as questions the reviewer can answer from the diff or a
targeted test, for example:

- Does the default remain unchanged when the new variable is unset?
- Can the deployment method actually pass the variable into the affected container?
- Is the browser calling the service directly, or should the gateway keep the request same-origin?

### Recommendation

End with one of:

- **Approve:** no blocking issue found and validation matches the risk.
- **Request changes:** name the blocking finding.
- **Needs context:** name the decision or evidence still required.

Keep the recommendation proportional to the inspection performed.

## Clarity rules

- Start from what a person sees, not from framework terminology.
- Define unavoidable terms on first use. For example: "CORS is the browser rule that controls
  requests to a different address."
- Use concrete ports, URLs, request paths, payloads, and environment variables when available.
- Use one idea per sentence.
- Distinguish fact from inference.
- Do not say "the web server calls the service" when the browser makes the request.
- If the user says they do not understand, make the model simpler. Do not repeat the same wording.
- Prefer a short diagram over a long architecture paragraph.
- Avoid generic approval language such as "small and safe" without explaining why.

## Quality check

Before responding, verify:

- The summary matches the diff, not only the PR description.
- Every named system has a clear role.
- The before/after behavior is concrete.
- Every risk has a condition and impact.
- Intent and implementation were judged separately.
- Failed checks were inspected before being classified.
- Existing review comments were verified after an independent pass.
- The recommendation follows from the findings and evidence.
- A reader unfamiliar with the subsystem can explain why the change is needed after reading the
  briefing.

skills.name: resolve-findings
skills.desc: Resolve findings by implementing the chosen fix path in code, tests, or docs. Accept optional `path` and a `priority` selector; by default resolve only the next highest remaining priority bucket, in order `P0`, `P1`, `P2`, `P3`. Also accept explicit levels or `all`. Default to `path=infer`. Confirm effective variables before starting.
skills.body:
---
name: resolve-findings
description: Resolve findings by implementing the chosen fix path in code, tests, or docs. Accept optional `path` and a `priority` selector; by default resolve only the next highest remaining priority bucket, in order `P0`, `P1`, `P2`, `P3`. Also accept explicit levels or `all`. Default to `path=infer`. Confirm effective variables before starting.
---

# Resolve Findings

Read these shared references when needed:

- `../shared/references/findings.schema.md`
- `../shared/references/findings.lifecycle.md`

## Role

Resolve is execution mode from findings back into code, tests, and docs.

- It may change production code for verification findings.
- It may change tests or test harnesses for validation findings.
- It should update the active findings record after implementation and rerun targeted checks when feasible.

## Priority Input

Accept a `priority` parameter from the prompt:

- omitted priority: resolve the next highest remaining bucket only
- explicit level: `P0`, `P1`, `P2`, or `P3`
- `all`: resolve all remaining buckets

Default:

- `priority=next-highest`

## Path Input

Accept an optional `path` from the prompt.

- If `path` is provided, use it as the local design or findings folder.
- If `path` is omitted, infer it from the branch, subsystem, or matching docs and state the inferred value before starting.

Default:

- `path=infer`

## Workflow

1. Determine the selected bucket.
   Confirm the effective variables first:
   - `path`
   - `priority`
   - target findings files when inferable

   Use the requested `priority`, or the next highest unresolved bucket in the active findings record.

2. Load the active findings record.
   Use `path/findings.md`.

3. Check readiness before coding.
   If the intended resolution path, policy boundary, or data contract is still ambiguous, ask the next follow-up question before editing.

4. Implement the selected fixes.
   Make the smallest coherent set of code, test, and doc changes needed for the selected findings bucket.

5. Re-run targeted checks.
   Use the narrowest useful verification or validation pass that demonstrates the fix.

6. Update the findings record.
   Move findings between open and closed sections, preserve notes and open questions ordering, and record what was fixed or what remains blocked.

## Rules

- Do not hide ambiguity behind `open` or `needs-user-decision` when the user already started answering. Ask the next concrete question.
- Do not silently widen scope from the selected priority bucket unless the fix is tightly coupled.

skills.name: review-correctness
skills.desc: Review one code change for correctness and rate it Low, Medium, or High. Looks for bugs, regressions in existing behavior, broken flows, concurrency and retry problems, and migrations that can fail or lose data. Use when asked to "review this PR for bugs", "check this diff for regressions", "is this change correct", or when a review loop runs the correctness lens. Read-only; it reports findings and does not fix them.
skills.body:
---
name: review-correctness
description: Review one code change for correctness and rate it Low, Medium, or High. Looks for bugs, regressions in existing behavior, broken flows, concurrency and retry problems, and migrations that can fail or lose data. Use when asked to "review this PR for bugs", "check this diff for regressions", "is this change correct", or when a review loop runs the correctness lens. Read-only; it reports findings and does not fix them.
---

# Review a change for correctness

You review one change and report what it breaks or can break, and how much it matters. You
do not edit code, and you do not post anything.

## Inputs

The caller gives you these. If the caller leaves one out, work it out and say what you used.

- **Checkout path.** A checkout of the repo at the head commit. Read code there.
- **Base.** The commit the change starts from. For a PR, use the merge base of the PR head
  and its base branch, never the current tip of the base branch.
- **Head.** The last commit of the change.
- **Context file (optional).** Decisions that are already settled: findings that were fixed,
  rejected with a reason, or deferred, and product rules from the owner. Do not raise a
  settled point again unless the fix is wrong or incomplete. Then say why.

Read the change with `git -C <checkout> diff <base> <head>`. Add `-- <path>` to read one file.

## What to look for

Read `lens.md` in this skill's directory and apply it.

## Rules

- Read-only. Do not install dependencies, and do not run builds, type checks, linters, or
  tests. Judge tests by reading them next to the code they test.
- Judge the final diff, not the commit history.
- Do not charge the change for problems in code it does not touch, unless the change makes
  an existing problem reachable.
- Raise a finding only with a concrete trigger you can reach. Say which input, state, or
  timing reaches it. Mark a finding you could not confirm as a hypothesis, and say what
  would confirm it.

## Output format

Write the report in plain English, in exactly this shape:

```markdown
# Correctness review
```

# Review a change or a design for naming and consistency

You review one target and report where names, patterns and layers are inconsistent, and how
much it matters. You do not edit code or documents, and you do not post anything. The rules
live in the `naming-and-resources` skill; this lens applies them.

## Targets

The caller names one target.

- **Code (default).** A diff between two commits that changes a contract: a table, column,
  index, route, DTO field, enum value, config field or UI label.
- **Design.** An OpenSpec change folder, a spec draft or an architecture doc. No code exists
  yet, or the code is not the subject. Check the proposal before any migration is written.
  When the doc describes existing code (an architecture map), review the names in the code
  it describes: folders, tables, modules, routes, types. The doc is the map, not the target.

## Inputs

The caller gives you these. If the caller leaves one out, work it out and say what you used.

For a code target: **checkout path** (the repo at the head commit), **base** (for a PR, the
merge base of the head and its base branch), **head**. Read the change with
`git -C <checkout> diff <base> <head>`.

For a design target: **checkout path** (today's code, to check what the design says about
today), **design path** (read every file), **version** (commit or date).

For both: **context file (optional)** with settled decisions and owner rules. Do not raise a
settled point again unless the fix is wrong or incomplete; then say why. Only the caller's
context file settles a point. A decision log inside the target (for example a `SETTLED.md`
in the spec folder) is part of the design under review: you may disagree with a naming
decision recorded there, cite the rule, and say where it was decided.

## Procedure

1. **Read the conventions first.** Read `lens.md` in this skill's directory, then from
   `.agents/skills/naming-and-resources/references/`: `project-conventions.md`,
   `naming-rules.md`, `layer-name-table.md`, `resource-template.md`. Read the `AGENTS.md` of
   each area the target touches and any glossary the target has. Read
   `references/calibration.md` for what is and is not a finding. Judge against these, not
   against a generic ideal. Flag a doc that the code contradicts.
2. **Sketch the path under review.** Write a few rows that give each module, its promise to
   callers, the details it keeps inside, the state it owns and its word for each concept. Share
   the sketch only when a finding needs it.
3. **Build the name inventory.** For each concept the target adds or changes, collect its
   name in every layer (the per-layer name table). Include enum values, index names, folder
   names, route parameters and UI labels. Collect every meaning of each word.
4. **Trace one normal path and one failure path** through every layer, from entry point to
   stored state and response, and check the name at each hop. For a design, follow the
   proposal step by step, and say that the result is reasoning rather than a test.
5. **Try one likely change.** Use a change that today's requirements make realistic (for
   example, one more item kind or one more owner level). Count the files it touches and the
   names it forces you to choose. Leave out consumers nobody has asked for.
6. **Apply the checks** in `references/checks.md`.
7. **Filter.** Pass each finding through the evidence gate in `references/report-template.md`.
   Group symptoms under one cause.
8. **Write the report** in the format of `references/report-template.md`, with the rating.

## Rules

- Read-only. Do not install dependencies, and do not run builds, type checks, linters, or
  tests.
- Review the target. Existing code counts where the target adds to it, copies it, or depends
  on it. A pre-existing mismatch that the target spreads to new surface is the target's.
- Project conventions win over generic standards. Never ask to move toward a generic rule
  that `project-conventions.md` overrides.
- Prefer a few substantial findings to a list of nits.
- Stay in this lens. Races and data loss go to review-correctness, removable parts and
  needless machinery to review-simplify, secrets and access to a security review, and field
  grouping by role to design-interfaces. Report the naming side of such an issue only. Drop
  a finding that sits fully in another lens.
- With a pull-request procedure (a review loop), the procedure owns the target, the head and
  publication. This lens writes its own report; the loop merges it into one findings list.
- Do not read `references/evals.md` during a review. It is for testing this skill.

## Optional references

Load only when needed:

- `references/optional/red-flags.md`: a one-page list of design warning signs, when a finding
  needs a short name for a structural problem.
- `references/optional/confidence-labels.md`: when the caller asks for a confidence label
  on each finding.
- `references/optional/action-timing.md`: when the caller asks when to act on each finding.
- `references/optional/long-report.md`: when the caller wants a full report instead of the
  lens format, for example a standalone architecture review.
- `references/optional/restraint-cases.md`: extra cases for when you are unsure whether a
  pattern is a real finding.

## Rating

- **Low:** names and patterns match the glossary, the conventions and the template, or only
  optional suggestions remain.
- **Medium:** on new surface, at least one concept has two names across layers, one word
  has two meanings, an item kind or an owner level breaks the shared template, or a layering
  fault adds a real obligation. The change still works.
- **High:** a mismatch on a shipped or about-to-ship contract (stored data, a migration, a
  public route or SDK field) that will need a migration to fix, or a name that leads callers
  to a wrong result.

The report ends with the line `Rating: Low|Medium|High` with nothing after it.

Looks for scope that could be narrower, edge cases that do not deserve machinery, state kept in several places, boundaries that only forward, and code or design parts whose reason to exist is gone. # Review a change or a design for simplicity

You review one target and report what could be removed or made simpler, and how much it
matters. You do not edit code or documents, and you do not post anything.

## Targets

The caller names one target.

- **Code (default).** A diff between two commits.
- **Design.** An OpenSpec change folder (`openspec/changes/<name>/`: proposal, design,
  specs, tasks) or one architecture doc. No code exists yet, or the code is not the subject.

## Inputs

The caller gives you these. If the caller leaves one out, work it out and say what you used.

For a code target:

- **Checkout path.** A checkout of the repo at the head commit. Read code there.
- **Base.** The commit the change starts from. For a PR, use the merge base of the PR head
  and its base branch, never the current tip of the base branch.
- **Head.** The last commit of the change.

Read the change with `git -C <checkout> diff <base> <head>`. Add `-- <path>` to read one file.

For a design target:

- **Checkout path.** A checkout of the repo the design applies to. Read today's code there,
  so you can check what the design claims about today and what it would add.
- **Design path.** The spec folder or the doc. Read every file in it.
- **Version.** The commit or date of the design, so the report names what you read.

For both:

- **Context file (optional).** Decisions that are already settled: findings that were fixed,
  rejected with a reason, or deferred, and product rules from the owner. Do not raise a
  settled point again unless the fix is wrong or incomplete. Then say why.

## What to look for

Read `lens.md` in this skill's directory and apply it. It explains how to judge scope, edge
cases, coordination, and the shape of the code.

For a design target, apply the lens to what the design would build:

- Scope. Compare the user outcome in the proposal with the mechanism in the design. Name a
  narrower contract that meets the same outcome.
- Requirements and scenarios that add machinery for a rare case. Ask whether a documented
  limit or a refusal is enough.
- New stores, flags, services, queues, settings, or routes. Ask whether existing state or an
  existing component can do the job.
- Interfaces. Fields that copy each other, or a boundary that only forwards.
- Tasks. Work whose only purpose is to support a part you suggest removing.

## Rules

- Read-only. Do not install dependencies, and do not run builds, type checks, linters, or
  tests.
- Review the target, not the code around it. Existing code counts only where the target adds
  to it or depends on it.
- Prefer a few substantial findings to a list of style nits.
- Keep a design when it is already the simplest one that meets the need, and say so.

## Rating

- **Low:** nothing to simplify, or only optional suggestions that the owner can take or leave.
- **Medium:** at least one simplification that removes a real obligation, such as a copy of
  state to keep in sync, a mode or route nobody needs, or a duplicate of an existing system.
  The change is still sound without it.
- **High:** the core approach carries complexity that much of the change should not have,
  or the complexity hides a correctness or reliability problem with a reachable trigger.

## Output format

Write the report in plain English, in exactly this shape:

```markdown
# Simplify review

Base: <base sha, or "design" for a design target>
Head: <head sha, or "<design path> at <commit or date>" for a design target>

## Findings

### 1. <one-line title>
- Severity: High | Medium | Low
- Where: <file>:<line> (more locations if needed; for a design, the spec file and heading)
- What is wrong: <what could disappear, and why the result is easier to reason about>
- Smallest fix: <the smallest change, and what behavior or tradeoff it changes>

(more findings, most important first; write "No findings." if there are none)

## What to keep

<parts of the design that are already simple and should stay; optional>

Rating: Low | Medium | High
```

Severity Low means a suggestion the owner may decline. The last line must be
`Rating: <value>` with nothing after it, so a script can read it.

  tests. Judge tests by reading them next to the code they test.
- Judge the final diff, not the commit history.
- Do not charge the change for problems in code it does not touch.
- Raise a finding only with a concrete trigger you can reach, or a clear maintenance cost.

## Output format

Write the report in plain English, in exactly this shape:

```markdown
# Slop review

Base: <base sha>
Head: <head sha>

## Findings

### 1. <one-line title>
- Severity: High | Medium | Low
- Where: <file>:<line> (more locations if needed)
- What is wrong: <the behavior or maintenance problem, and how to reach it>
- Smallest fix: <the smallest change that removes the problem>

(more findings, most severe first; write "No findings." if there are none)

## Rationale

<the two strongest reasons for the rating, as concrete behavior or architecture problems>

Rating: Low | Medium | High
```

The last line must be `Rating: <value>` with nothing after it, so a script can read it.

---
name: style-editing
description: Apply Joseph Williams' clarity principles when writing or editing prose. Use when drafting technical or business writing, diagnosing unclear sentences, rewriting passive or abstract prose, or any time the user references Williams, "Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace," or "Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace."
---

# Williams' Style: Clarity and Grace

Practical principles from Joseph M. Williams' *Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace* (and the condensed *Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace*). Use as a checklist when writing or editing prose that needs to be clear, direct, and reader-friendly.

## Core philosophy

Williams' two foundational claims:
1. It is good to write clearly.
2. Anyone can write clearly, if they revise with the right principles in mind.

Skilled writers don't *write* clear sentences. They *revise into* them. Treat first drafts as raw material. Apply these principles in revision passes.

Clarity is reader-first: your job is to make the reader's work easy.

## The two foundational principles

### 1. Characters as subjects, actions as verbs

The grammatical subject of a sentence should name the actual character (the agent doing something). The verb should name what that character does.

When the subject is an abstraction and the verb is weak, the sentence loses energy and clarity.

- Bad: *"There was a decision by the committee to approve the budget."*
- Good: *"The committee decided to approve the budget."*

- Bad: *"The intention of the team was the implementation of a new policy."*
- Good: *"The team intended to implement a new policy."*

Diagnostic question for any unclear sentence: **Who is doing what?** If the answer is buried in nouns and prepositions, rewrite so the actor is the subject and the action is the verb.

### 2. Avoid nominalizations

A nominalization is a verb (or adjective) converted into a noun. They drain action from prose.

Common signs:
- Words ending in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -al, -ity, -ness in subject position
- Phrases like "make a decision," "conduct an analysis," "give consideration to"

Rewrites:
- "Make a decision" → "decide"
- "Conduct an analysis of" → "analyze"
- "Give consideration to" → "consider"
- "Reach an agreement" → "agree"
- "Have a discussion about" → "discuss"

When you spot a nominalization in subject or object position, ask: can I turn it back into a verb and find a real character to do it?

## Voice and emphasis

### 3. Active over passive (with exceptions)

Default to active voice. Use passive only when:
- The agent is unknown ("My car was stolen.")
- The agent is unimportant or obvious
- You need to keep the subject consistent across sentences (cohesion — see below)
- You want to put the agent at the end of the sentence for emphasis (stress position)

Active voice puts the character first, where the reader expects to find it.

### 4. Stress position: end of sentence carries weight

Readers feel the natural emphasis of a sentence at its end. Put the most important new information there.

- Weak: *"Climate change is the most pressing issue facing humanity, in my opinion."*
- Strong: *"In my opinion, the most pressing issue facing humanity is climate change."*

- Weak: *"Agenta is the AI reliability layer that closes that gap, fundamentally."*
- Strong: *"The gap is what Agenta closes."*

When revising, ask: what's the most important word or idea in this sentence? Is it landing in the stress position?

## Cohesion across sentences

### 5. Old before new

Each sentence should start with information the reader already knows (from the previous sentence or shared context) and end with new information. This creates a chain readers can follow effortlessly.

- Choppy: *"Photosynthesis converts sunlight to energy. The Calvin cycle is the second stage of photosynthesis. Carbon fixation happens in the Calvin cycle."*
- Cohesive: *"Photosynthesis converts sunlight to energy. The second stage of photosynthesis is the Calvin cycle, which fixes carbon."*

In the cohesive version, each sentence picks up where the last one left off.

### 6. Topic strings (consistent subjects across a paragraph)

A paragraph has a "topic string" — the chain of grammatical subjects across its sentences. When the topic string is consistent, the paragraph feels unified. When subjects keep changing, the paragraph feels scattered.

Diagnostic: list the grammatical subject of each sentence in the paragraph. If the list is "team / data / system / users / process / our approach," the paragraph has no topic string. Pick one anchor character (often the most important agent in the paragraph) and rewrite so most sentences share that subject.

This is what passive voice is good for: it lets you keep the same subject across sentences even when the action changes hands.

### 7. Topic + body + close in paragraphs

Each paragraph should:
- Open with a controlling sentence (the issue or claim)
- Develop it in the body
- Close with a sentence that points forward, names the consequence, or summarises

Don't bury the controlling idea in the middle. The opening sets the topic; the close earns the stress position.

## Concision

### 8. Cut what you don't need

Williams' favourite categories of cuts:

**Wordy phrases:**
- "due to the fact that" → "because"
- "in order to" → "to"
- "at this point in time" → "now"
- "for the purpose of" → "to"
- "in the event that" → "if"
- "with regard to" → "about"
- "the fact that" → usually deletable

**Doublets** (keep one of each pair):
- "each and every"
- "first and foremost"
- "any and all"
- "true and accurate"

**Empty modifiers:**
- very, really, basically, actually, literally, essentially, simply, quite, rather

**Throat-clearing openers:**
- "I think that..."
- "It should be noted that..."
- "It is important to remember that..."

**Redundant pairs:**
- "free gift" (gifts are free)
- "advance planning" (planning is in advance)
- "end result" (results are at the end)

### 9. Sentence length: vary it on purpose

Mix short and long sentences. A short sentence after a long one creates emphasis. A run of short sentences in a row gets choppy. A run of long sentences in a row gets exhausting.

Read your prose aloud. The rhythm should breathe.

## Grace (the optional layer)

### 10. Parallel structure

When you list or contrast, use parallel grammatical structure so the reader sees the parallel meaning.

- Bad: *"She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike."*
- Good: *"She likes hiking, swimming, and biking."*

- Bad: *"The product is fast, reliable, and you can scale it."*
- Good: *"The product is fast, reliable, and scalable."*

### 11. Balanced sentences

Two parallel halves separated by a comma, semicolon, or colon create rhythm and emphasis.

- *"Demos are easy. Reliability isn't."*
- *"They iterate on prompts; the system iterates on them."*

Use sparingly. Overused, balance becomes mannered.

### 12. End on the strongest word

When you have a choice, arrange the sentence so the strongest word lands last. The reader's ear hears it as the point.

## Ethics

### 13. Write to others as you'd want them to write to you

Avoid:
- Jargon that excludes readers who don't share your specialty
- Hedges that obscure responsibility ("mistakes were made")
- Complexity used to signal authority rather than clarify
- Vague language that lets you avoid commitment

If you'd be frustrated reading what you've written, revise.

## A working diagnostic checklist

When editing a draft, run through:

1. **Subject test.** What is the grammatical subject of each sentence in the paragraph? Is there a topic string? If not, pick an anchor character and rewrite.
2. **Verb test.** Are the verbs concrete actions, or weak constructions ("is," "has," "makes," "does")? Look for nominalizations to convert back to verbs.
3. **Voice test.** Each passive sentence: is it passive for a reason? If not, flip to active.
4. **Stress position test.** What word ends each sentence? Is it the most important word, or a throwaway?
5. **Cut test.** Read each sentence and ask: which words can I delete without losing meaning? Cut them.
6. **Length test.** Read aloud. Does the rhythm vary? Do any sentences run on or chop short without purpose?
7. **Reader test.** If you were the reader, would you understand this on first read?

## When to apply this skill

- Drafting any prose where clarity matters: technical writing, sales copy, internal memos, exec summaries, blog posts, documentation
- Editing or revising prose that feels dense, abstract, or passive
- Diagnosing why a paragraph feels off
- When the user references Williams, *Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace*, *Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace*, "old-before-new," "topic string," or "stress position"

This skill complements `ai-writing-tropes` (which lists patterns to avoid). Williams gives the positive principles; tropes gives the negative ones.

## Sources

- Williams, Joseph M. and Bizup, Joseph. *Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace*. (Ten editions, the foundational text.)
- Williams, Joseph M. *Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace*. (Condensed, paperback companion.)
- Williams, Joseph M. *Style: Toward Clarity and Grace*. (Earlier title in the same family.)

skills.name: sync-findings
skills.desc: Sync the findings record against local review artifacts and optionally a GitHub PR. Accept optional `path` and GitHub PR `url`; when `url` is provided, sync against both remote PR state and local state, otherwise default to local-only sync. Default to `path=infer`. Confirm effective variables before starting.
skills.body:
---
name: sync-findings
description: Sync the findings record against local review artifacts and optionally a GitHub PR. Accept optional `path` and GitHub PR `url`; when `url` is provided, sync against both remote PR state and local state, otherwise default to local-only sync. Default to `path=infer`. Confirm effective variables before starting.
---

# Sync Findings

Read these shared references when needed:

- `../shared/references/findings.schema.md`
- `../shared/references/findings.lifecycle.md`

## Role

Keep the active findings record aligned with current local state and, when requested, current GitHub PR state.

- Pull in open PR comments, review notes, local review docs, and current code state.
- Map comments to findings, update sources and statuses, and surface follow-up questions.
- When GitHub thread operations are available, reply to and resolve threads that are clearly closed by current findings.

## URL Input

Accept an optional GitHub PR `url` from the prompt.

- If a PR URL is provided, do remote plus local sync.
- If no URL is provided, do local-only sync.

Default:

- `url=local-only`

## Path Input

Accept an optional `path` from the prompt.

- If `path` is provided, use it as the local design or findings folder.
- If `path` is omitted, infer it from the branch, subsystem, or matching docs and state the inferred value before starting.

Default:

- `path=infer`

## Workflow

1. Establish sync scope.
   Confirm the effective variables first:
   - `path`
   - `url`
   - branch, PR URL if present, and any requested focus areas

2. Load the active findings record.
   Use `path/findings.md`.

3. **SAVE FIRST — write every new finding into `path/findings.md` before doing anything else.**
   This is the non-negotiable first action of every sync. Before proposing fixes, discussing implications, replying to threads, or updating any other doc:
   - For each new PR review comment or scan observation, add an entry under `## Open Findings` using the canonical schema (ID, severity, files, evidence, decision pending).
   - Mark every new finding as `needs-user-decision` unless the user has already given direction.
   - Refresh the `## Summary` section so the latest state is visible at the top.
   - Only after `findings.md` is up to date may you start summarizing for the user or proposing fixes.

   This rule exists because diving straight into "let me explain / propose / fix" mode loses context and leaves the user to reconstruct the finding list themselves. The doc is the source of truth, not the chat history.

4. Sync sources into findings.
   Re-check existing findings against current local code and docs.
   If `url` is present, pull open PR comments and thread state into the same record.

5. Ask clarifying questions before parking ambiguity.
   If a finding's disposition or intended action is still unclear, ask the next concrete question instead of silently leaving it vague.

6. Close only what is clearly closed.
   When a GitHub thread maps to a closed finding, leave a short reply with the finding ID when relevant and resolve the thread.
   Leave still-open or still-ambiguous threads untouched.

## Rules

- **Save-first is mandatory.** Step 3 must complete before any code change, fix proposal, GitHub reply, or summary update. No exceptions.
- Sync is not a substitute for execution planning; use `triage-findings` when the user needs help deciding what to do next.
- Do not silently drop sources, thread IDs, or comment provenance.
