skills.name: write-whats-new
skills.desc: Write the in-app "What's new" copy and the matching docs changelog entry for an Agenta release, the way Mahmoud approves it the first time. Covers the title, the summary, lists of models, improvements and fixes, what to leave out, and the cover picture. Use when writing or reviewing a changelog entry for a version, the What's new dialog text, or release notes that people read in the app.
skills.body:
---
name: write-whats-new
description: Write the in-app "What's new" copy and the matching docs changelog entry for an Agenta release, the way Mahmoud approves it the first time. Covers the title, the summary, lists of models, improvements and fixes, what to leave out, and the cover picture. Use when writing or reviewing a changelog entry for a version, the What's new dialog text, or release notes that people read in the app.
---

# Write the What's new copy

The "What's new" dialog in `/m` (`web/mobile/src/features/education/WhatsNewDialog.tsx`) opens on
Home when a release came out that the browser has not seen. Its text comes from the docs
changelog entries in `docs/blog/entries/*.mdx`: the `<Summary>` block, the `improvements` and
`fixes` lists in the frontmatter, and the `cover` field. `pnpm generate:releases` in `web/`
builds `web/packages/agenta-navigation/src/releases/changelog.json` from them. Do not hand-edit
that file.

The procedure for the docs page itself (slug, frontmatter, `<Summary>`, `{/* truncate */}`, the
full write-up) is in the `create-changelog-announcement` skill. This skill sets how the text
reads.

## Write for the person who uses the app

- Say what the person can now do, and why it helps them. Do not describe how it works inside.
  Before: "The runner reuses local tool binaries and a harness capability probe."
  After: "Agent chats start faster."
- Use the names the app shows: screen names, button labels, model names as the model picker
  shows them. Bold a button or screen name: **Settings**, **Builder**.
- Leave out internal names: runner, harness (Pi, Codex, Claude Code as a harness), spans,
  baggage, Composio, library names such as pypdf, ids, env vars.
- Call the builder "the builder agent" the first time, then "the builder".
- Do not describe UI mechanics that people see anyway, such as "each change shows as a card".

## The parts of one entry

1. **Title.** What the person gets, in plain words. The timeline row in the dialog shows about
   26 characters, so put the meaning in the first words. Examples that were approved:
   "Meet the builder agent", "New models for your agents",
   "Discord, Microsoft Teams and localization".
2. **Summary.** One or two short paragraphs. Start with what changed for the person, then where
   to find it, then what it can do. A closing line such as "We will keep making it better" is
   fine for a new feature.
3. **Lists, not sentences, for many names.** When a release adds models, list each model on
   its own line, grouped by how the person pays for it:
   - "Built-in models, paid with your Agenta credits like the other built-in models. You need
     no key of your own:" then the list.
   - "With your own provider key or subscription:" then the list.
   Write the full model name ("Claude Fable 5.2", "GPT-6.2 Sol"). Never name the harness.
4. **Improvements and fixes.** One line each, with an area label (Agents, Automations,
   Sessions, Integrations, Phone). Say what the person sees. A change that makes something
   work as it should is a fix, not an improvement (for example "Codex now asks before it edits
   a file when the tool policy says to ask").

## Leave out

- Dependency and security version bumps ("Updated Next.js and Hono"). They are not useful to
  the reader.
- Features that have no place in the app's screens yet. Announce them when the UI ships. (Shared
  drives shipped in v0.129.0 without a UI, so no entry names them yet.)
- Small setting removals that nobody asked for (for example removed developer switches).
- Self-hosting upgrade steps. They stay in the full docs page, not in the summary.

## Cover

Every new entry gets a cover above its title. Mahmoud likes covers. Build them from pictures the
app already has, never from new art:

- Channel logos from `web/packages/agenta-settings-ui/src/channels/icons.tsx`
  (Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Teams).
- Model provider logos from `web/packages/agenta-ui/src/LLMIcons/` (Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI,
  Mistral and others), next to chips with the model names.
- The builder's ribbon animation (`web/mobile/src/features/builder-page/hero/`).
- Language names as chips, each in its own language.

Set the cover in the entry's frontmatter (`cover: channels`, `models`, `builder`, ...). A demo
video (`streamVideoId`) replaces the cover when the entry has one. A new kind of cover needs one
small component in `web/mobile/src/features/education/`.

## Review before you show Mahmoud

- Put the dialog on an artifact page, today and proposed side by side, with the real `/m`
  tokens, so he can comment per entry. Count the title characters and mark the ones the
  timeline cuts.
- Read each line as a user who has never seen the code. If a line needs the code to make sense,
  rewrite it or drop it.
- Check each claim against the code or the PR. For example, do not say the builder "creates
  automations" while its instructions say it cannot.

skills.name: agenta-apps
skills.desc: How to give the person a small interactive page in the drive: a board, checklist, queue, form, table or dashboard. Read it when the ask is for something to look at and touch rather than a reply. Covers picking a starter with create_app, the app folder layout, and the window.agenta bridge for hand-written apps.
skills.body:
---
name: agenta-apps
description: >-
  How to give the person a small interactive page in the drive: a board, checklist, queue, form, table or dashboard. Read it when the ask is for something to look at and touch rather than a reply. Covers picking a starter with create_app, the app folder layout, and the window.agenta bridge for hand-written apps.
---
# Agenta apps

## When

The person asks for something to look at and touch rather than a reply: a board, a checklist,
a queue, a form, a table, a small dashboard. Build an app folder in the drive; the drive renders
it in a sandboxed page and shows it as a card in the chat. Do not build one for a one-off answer.

## First

1. List `apps/*/app.json`. If an app already covers the ask, update its files; never make a
   second copy of the same app.
2. Pick a starter from the table below and call `create_app(starter, "apps/<slug>")`. Then write
   its config file and, when the person gave you content, its data file.

   sweep), propose a schedule in Triggers when you have `create_schedule`. Say plainly that a
   scheduled run writes into its own session, not this one, so the app will not refresh itself
   here: the person reopens it after a run, or asks you to copy the new data across. Apps live
   in the session drive; `create_app` cannot write to `agent-files/`, so do not offer to put one

skills.name: tavily-job-search
skills.desc: Use when searching the web for job openings, comparing job-board search strategies, validating listings, and extracting job details with Tavily.
skills.body:
---
name: tavily-job-search
description: Use when searching the web for job openings, comparing job-board search strategies, validating listings, and extracting job details with Tavily.
---

# Tavily Job Search and Page Extraction

Use this skill to discover job openings with Tavily, compare sources, verify relevance, and extract useful details from shortlisted postings. Tavily is web search and extraction, not a structured jobs API: results can be duplicated, stale, mislocated, incomplete, or mixed with recommendations and similar jobs. Verify each posting rather than treating a query result as authoritative.

## 1. Build focused searches

1. Start with the target title, city, and country in the query, such as `Data Engineer jobs Berlin Germany`. Use role variants when useful: `Senior Data Engineer`, `Data Platform Engineer`, `Analytics Engineer`; add local-language variants where relevant (for Munich, try both `Munich` and `München`).
2. Search distinct source groups separately so source quality and noise are visible. Use `search_depth: "advanced"`, `max_results: 10`, and an explicit country name for the `country` boost:
   - Aggregators and tech boards: `include_domains: ["startup.jobs", "wellfound.com", "builtin.com", "englishjobs.de"]`.
   - LinkedIn: `include_domains: ["linkedin.com"]`.
   - Indeed: `include_domains: ["indeed.com"]`; optionally test a country-specific host such as `de.indeed.com`.
   Keep the actual query explicit about city + country even when `country` is set.
3. Run multiple city/role combinations independently. For example, Berlin + Data Engineer, Munich + Machine Learning Engineer, and Amsterdam + Backend Engineer. If a week filter returns too few viable roles, widen `time_range` to `month` or remove it, then verify each role is still open from the posting or official careers page.
4. Treat `country` as a relevance boost, not a strict geographic filter. `include_domains` restricts the source domain, not the job location. A country-specific Indeed hostname did not remove unrelated roles. In testing, `exact_match: true` on a quoted title did not reliably eliminate geographic noise either; use it only as a query precision experiment, never as a substitute for checking the location.

## 2. Screen and verify the search results

For each candidate, inspect the result's title, URL, snippet, and the text of the posting itself. Keep only roles whose actual location or eligible remote region matches the user's target. Do not infer location from the query page or a “similar jobs” section. For example, Berlin may mean Berlin, Germany or a U.S. town such as Berlin, Connecticut or Massachusetts; a result labelled “Berlin, Free State” needs corroborating context before inclusion.

Check and record:

- Exact title, employer, location / remote eligibility, and employment type when shown.
- Posting date, deadline, and whether the role is still accepting applications. A recent search result is not proof that a posting is open; pages can say removed, expired, or no longer accepting applications.
- Whether the page is the actual vacancy or only a results/category page containing a matching snippet.
- Duplicate postings across aggregators and LinkedIn/Indeed. Deduplicate by employer + normalized title + location, preferring the employer's own active careers page as the canonical apply link.

LinkedIn often returns broad EEA/DACH or remote roles and many adjacent “similar jobs.” Its page can still expose useful role details and a named recruiter/job poster; verify that the person and contact information belong to the exact vacancy. Indeed can surface valid roles but also wrong-country mirrors and irrelevant snippets. A Germany-only host may reduce some domain noise, but it is not a location filter.

## 3. Extract shortlisted postings

After screening, call the available Tavily extract tool on a small shortlist (typically 3–5 direct posting URLs), using `extract_depth: "advanced"`, `format: "markdown"`, and a focused query, for example:

`Extract the exact role title, employer, location, posting/deadline/status, responsibilities, required and preferred skills, salary, team context, named hiring contact, and apply URL.`

Extraction is uneven by source. In testing, a LinkedIn Booking.com posting yielded responsibilities and requirements; a LinkedIn recruiter post exposed a recruiter's name and technical requirements; an aggregator page returned only a partial job summary; a direct Indeed posting failed to fetch. When extraction fails or is partial:

1. Keep the failure explicit; do not fill missing details from assumptions.
2. Use the Tavily search snippet as a lead, not as verified page content.
3. Search the exact title + employer and look for the employer's own careers page; extract that canonical page if available.
4. If no authoritative source can be reached, mark the field unknown and retain the third-party URL only as a lead.

For company/team research, run separate targeted searches or Tavily research after selecting the actual jobs. Seek official product, careers, engineering/blog, team, and recent-news pages. Attribute facts to the source URL and distinguish directly published information from inference.

## 4. Recommended run shape

1. Search across the relevant source groups and role/city variants.
2. Merge and deduplicate candidates; verify geography, recency, and active status.
3. Extract only the best-matching direct job pages.
4. Research each employer and relevant team from public sources.
5. Produce a shortlist with apply links, evidence-backed fit notes, contact leads only when publicly named, and clear caveats for stale, incomplete, or unverified details.

Optimize for verified relevant opportunities, not raw result count. If the user explicitly asks for a broad lead list, show the noisy leads separately from verified matches.

# Prospect research

1. Read the confirmed target criteria before evaluating a company.

skills.name: content-briefing
skills.desc: Create or revise an evidence-backed SEO brief for owner approval before scaffolding or drafting.
skills.body:
---
name: "content-briefing"
description: "Create or revise an evidence-backed SEO brief for owner approval before scaffolding or drafting."
---

# Content briefing

## Goal
Turn an agreed content opportunity into a shared understanding of the page we want to make. A useful brief gives the writer direction and lets the owner correct the angle before time goes into drafting.

## Suggested approach
Read the relevant business or website context, research and existing content. Understand the reader's question and why this page would help. Check whether the task is a new page or an improvement to an existing one.

Develop the proposed angle, intended reader, main answer and distinctive contribution. Suggest an outline when it helps explain the approach, without prescribing every paragraph. Consider examples, product demonstrations or other evidence that will make the page convincing, along with useful links and a natural next step for the reader.

Adapt this to the page type and the owner's goals. A tutorial needs a working procedure; a comparison needs fair decision criteria; a personal or creative site may need a different treatment. Consult the relevant existing article playbook rather than imposing one format on all work.

Discuss missing information that would materially change the brief. Bring a concrete proposal to the owner and improve it through their feedback, rather than asking them to supply the entire assignment.

Brief approval requires the user question, site fit, required proof, next visitor action and owner. For SEO-led work, include a target query, search intent and observed demand evidence. For sharing-led or other non-search work, mark search demand as unproven or not applicable and explain the audience need instead. Explain these in language appropriate to the site; for a non-commercial project, fit and the next visitor action should reflect its purpose. Do not invent evidence to fill a field. Obtain owner approval of the actual brief before drafting.

## A useful brief format
Use this as a readable starting shape, not a form to fill mechanically. Keep the existing record metadata separate from the editorial proposal. A small update may need a short note; a new comparison usually needs more detail.

### Proposal
Give a working title, page type and whether this creates a page or updates an existing URL. In a short paragraph explain who the reader is, what they are trying to do, the main answer we intend to give, why this site can help and what this piece adds. State important boundaries so the writer knows what not to cover. Suggest a few genuinely different title/angle options only when a choice would help; recommend one.

### Search and audience evidence
For SEO-led work, name the target query, intended search intent and linked observed demand. Summarize representative current results and what they suggest about format, depth and unmet needs, with date/locale and capture limitations. Reuse planning research; refresh it when stale or when the angle changes. Keep related questions together when they support the same task rather than making a keyword quota. Explain how the proposal differs from existing site pages.

### Proposed structure
Give descriptive section headings with a sentence about the question each section answers. Note the key example, demonstration, comparison or source that belongs there. A heading list alone is often too vague; a nearly complete draft defeats the purpose of brief approval. Sequence the reader's questions rather than copying competitors' headings.

### Proof and assets
Connect consequential claims to available sources or planned verification. For example: 'Setup takes these steps: verify by running the documented workflow'; 'Supports private deployment: confirm current deployment documentation'; 'Saves time: needs a defined measurement, otherwise omit the quantified promise.' Distinguish evidence already held from work still required. Name needed screenshots, diagrams, datasets, interviews or runnable examples, what each should show, and any owner-supplied material. A planned test is not a passed test.

### Reader journey and decisions
Suggest useful existing internal links and a natural next action, such as trying the procedure, downloading a resource or reading the next guide. Include the owner and a short batch of decisions needed about angle, scope or proof. Make your recommendation first. Clearly state what is ready for approval and what missing evidence prevents it. Do not treat a casual topic selection as approval of this brief.

## Format-specific starting points
- **Tutorial:** promised outcome, audience prerequisites, environment, ordered steps, expected results, verification and likely troubleshooting. Plan a testable procedure before committing to claims. Link optional background rather than burying the steps under it.
- **Comparison or alternatives:** reader decision, fair selection criteria, compared entities, a summary table, comparable evidence for each option, best-fit scenarios and limitations. Plan how volatile facts such as pricing will be dated. Do not select criteria solely to make our product win.
- **Explainer or guide:** direct answer, essential concepts, a concrete example, important distinctions and next steps. Broader coverage is useful only when it serves the question; a glossary paragraph is not automatically a separate article.
- **Case study:** starting situation, constraints, intervention, observed results, measurement basis and lessons. Identify permission and evidence needs; do not invent quotes or attribute outcomes to the intervention without support.
- **Refresh:** existing URL, reason for change, sections to retain, specific changes, new proof and expected reader benefit. Preserve the page's identity and approved material outside the scope.

These shapes complement the applicable owner playbook, not replace it. Useful defaults are to settle the reader promise before polishing the title, identify hard-to-obtain proof early, and keep the outline flexible enough for discoveries during writing. If research undermines the proposed answer, revise the brief rather than force evidence to fit it.

## Tools and integrations
Existing knowledge and research notes provide the foundation. Use connected search or page-reading tools when a claim or angle needs further investigation. Store the brief with the existing content record so it remains connected to feedback and the eventual draft.

## Useful output
An understandable proposed assignment that the owner can discuss and approve. It should communicate the intended outcome, angle and important evidence, not become a rigid document completed for its own sake. Use the detail necessary for this piece; leave room for good writing decisions during production.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read the selected opportunity from its plan/Discovery, linked research and current Knowledge/voice notes. Link those inputs in the brief so the writer can revisit the reasoning.

For production-owned work, use agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/brief.md. For app-owned work, use agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/brief.md with existing content identity, frontmatter and related-record links. Determine which location owns the item; do not create both. Draft, feedback and assets belong beside the same brief. Keep approval references and feedback attached to the relevant version through the existing request procedure. Link raw research where it lives. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; label recovery snapshots as archives.

A heading list alone is often too vague; a nearly complete draft defeats the purpose of brief approval. Sequence the reader's questions rather than copying competitors' headings.

### Proof and assets
Connect consequential claims to available sources or planned verification. For example: 'Setup takes these steps: verify by running the documented workflow'; 'Supports private deployment: confirm current deployment documentation'; 'Saves time: needs a defined measurement, otherwise omit the quantified promise.' Distinguish evidence already held from work still required. Name needed screenshots, diagrams, datasets, interviews or runnable examples, what each should show, and any owner-supplied material. A planned test is not a passed test.

### Reader journey and decisions
Suggest useful existing internal links and a natural next action, such as trying the procedure, downloading a resource or reading the next guide. Include the owner and a short batch of decisions needed about angle, scope or proof. Make your recommendation first. Clearly state what is ready for approval and what missing evidence prevents it. Do not treat a casual topic selection as approval of this brief.

## Format-specific starting points
- **Tutorial:** promised outcome, audience prerequisites, environment, ordered steps, expected results, verification and likely troubleshooting. Plan a testable procedure before committing to claims. Link optional background rather than burying the steps under it.
- **Comparison or alternatives:** reader decision, fair selection criteria, compared entities, a summary table, comparable evidence for each option, best-fit scenarios and limitations. Plan how volatile facts such as pricing will be dated. Do not select criteria solely to make our product win.
- **Explainer or guide:** direct answer, essential concepts, a concrete example, important distinctions and next steps. Broader coverage is useful only when it serves the question; a glossary paragraph is not automatically a separate article.
- **Case study:** starting situation, constraints, intervention, observed results, measurement basis and lessons. Identify permission and evidence needs; do not invent quotes or attribute outcomes to the intervention without support.
- **Refresh:** existing URL, reason for change, sections to retain, specific changes, new proof and expected reader benefit. Preserve the page's identity and approved material outside the scope.

Useful defaults are to settle the reader promise before polishing the title, identify hard-to-obtain proof early, and keep the outline flexible enough for discoveries during writing. If research undermines the proposed answer, revise the brief rather than force evidence to fit it.

## Tools and integrations
Existing knowledge and research notes provide the foundation. Use connected search or page-reading tools when a claim or angle needs further investigation. Store the brief with the existing content record so it remains connected to feedback and the eventual draft.

## Useful output
An understandable proposed assignment that the owner can discuss and approve. It should communicate the intended outcome, angle and important evidence, not become a rigid document completed for its own sake. Use the detail necessary for this piece; leave room for good writing decisions during production.

For production-owned work, use agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/brief.md. For app-owned work, use agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/brief.md with existing content identity, frontmatter and related-record links. Determine which location owns the item; do not create both. Draft, feedback and assets belong beside the same brief. Keep approval references and feedback attached to the relevant version through the existing request procedure. Link raw research where it lives. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; label recovery snapshots as archives.

---
name: "content-planning"
description: "Prioritize content opportunities or a small cluster and decide create versus update from business fit, demand evidence, existing coverage and proof."
---

# Content planning

## Goal
Help the owner decide what content is worth making or improving, and why. Connect audience needs with the site's purpose, existing coverage and the kind of contribution the owner can genuinely make.

For a business, the desired result might be qualified inquiries or product use. For an artist, community or hobby site, it might be discovery, participation or sharing expertise. Use the owner's goals rather than assuming every page should sell something.

## Suggested approach
Start with current knowledge of the site and conversations with the owner. Review audience questions, demand research, existing pages and any available performance information. Ask about priorities or capacity when they would change the recommendation.

Look for opportunities to answer a real question well. Consider what the owner can add through experience, examples, tools, original work or a clearer explanation. Check whether an existing page could serve that need before proposing a new one.

Compare candidates using judgment about relevance, evidence of interest, distinct value, effort and the next action useful to the reader. Search volume can inform the choice but cannot establish fit on its own. Autocomplete suggests wording, not volume. Similar queries do not automatically mean existing pages are competing harmfully.

Explain the trade-offs instead of assigning unsupported numerical scores. Where evidence is thin, identify a useful investigation or ask the owner a focused question. Keep a proposed research topic distinct from a validated SEO target.

Recommend a manageable starting point and how related pieces might support it. For this agent's current workflow, keep the first cluster small so we can learn from actual results before expanding. Update the plan as owner feedback and outcomes change the picture.

## Practical planning methods

### Gather candidates from several kinds of evidence
Start with a small working set from existing research rather than an exhaustive keyword dump. Useful sources include repeated audience questions, support or sales conversations shared by the owner, relevant forum discussions, competitor topic/keyword research, and queries already earning impressions in Search Console. Keep the source beside each candidate. A customer question establishes an audience need, not necessarily search demand; a competitor post establishes coverage, not performance.

For supplied keyword exports, retain provider, date, country, ranking URL and metric definitions. Look for relevant question/use-case variations, competing page types and existing visibility. Difficulty and traffic estimates are clues, not promises. Without paid data, inspect public questions and search results and make qualitative recommendations with clear limits.

### Group by the reader's task, then check search intent
Group questions that one useful page could answer together. Use modifiers such as 'what is', 'how to', 'vs', 'alternatives', 'template' and 'examples' to form initial hypotheses about learning, choosing or implementing. Confirm against actual results and audience context; modifiers alone do not determine intent.

Read representative results for shortlisted queries. Notice whether searchers are being served tutorials, product pages, lists, tools, videos or discussions. Compare overlapping results and reader tasks before splitting similar keywords into separate pages. Do not assume every keyword needs a URL or every topic needs a long article. General web discovery is not a localized ranking capture; record what evidence was actually available.

### Map opportunities to existing pages
Compare the shortlist with the site's inventory, including relevant product, documentation and resource pages, not just its blog. Ask whether an existing page already serves the same reader and intent, whether it can be improved without distorting its purpose, and where a genuinely different need calls for a new page.

Where Search Console data is available, inspect query/page pairs with relevant impressions and weaker-than-expected results. Average positions around 8–20 can identify candidates to investigate, but are not automatic quick wins. Compare like periods, country/device and branded versus nonbranded queries; consider intent mismatch, SERP features and technical problems before prescribing more content. Aggregate position and CTR alone cannot establish the cause.

### State the contribution and choose the format
For each serious candidate, finish the sentence: 'This helps [reader] do [task], and adds [specific contribution] beyond the current options.' Useful contributions include a tested procedure, original example, owner experience, usable template, fair decision criteria or a clearer answer. If the contribution is vague, improve the angle or investigate proof before commissioning a generic rewrite.

Choose the format around the task: a tutorial for doing something, a comparison for a real choice, a template for producing an artifact, a case study for learning from an evidenced outcome. A hub helps when readers need orientation among several substantial resources; related standalone pages can work without a new hub or URL hierarchy. Original commentary may be valuable for sharing even when search demand is unproven—label that purpose rather than force an SEO justification.

### Compare options and sequence a small plan
Compare audience/site fit, observed demand, contribution, likely usefulness of the next visitor action, effort and maintenance burden. Use plain-language trade-offs; if numerical scoring is requested, expose the assumptions instead of treating arbitrary weights as evidence. Separate missing evidence from weak opportunity.

Assign a useful next action: create, update, investigate or defer. Explain why the first choice comes before the next, which evidence or assets it depends on, and what would change the order. Group essential owner questions about priorities, proof and capacity into one short batch rather than interrupting repeatedly.

Start with a small connected set, for example one main answer and two supporting pieces if each serves a distinct need. Link them where it helps the reader. Sequence by usefulness and dependencies, not a blanket rule that the hub must ship first. Suggest a realistic discovery/distribution route and what outcome to observe; a proposed newsletter or community post does not authorize sending it. Do not create a calendar or publishing cadence merely to fill slots.

## Useful priors, not universal rules
These are starting beliefs to revise with evidence, not measured probabilities:
- **Relevant needs usually beat raw volume.** A narrow question close to the owner's goals can be more valuable than a broad popular topic. Override when broad education is itself the goal or there is evidence it brings the right audience.
- **Improving a relevant existing page is often cheaper than making a near-duplicate.** Prefer investigating an update when the intent already matches. Create separately when the reader task genuinely differs; consolidation or URL changes require their own decision.
- **Repeated audience questions plus observed search demand are stronger than a keyword-tool suggestion alone.** Small or biased samples still need interpretation. Low reported volume does not prove no demand, especially for new or specialized topics.
- **Concrete experience and usable proof are promising advantages.** Prefer a topic we can demonstrate over one where we can only paraphrase competitors. This is a usefulness prior, not a ranking guarantee or a requirement to invent novelty.
- **Existing relevant impressions may offer a shorter feedback loop.** Inspect those pages before assuming new content is the best investment. Override when their intent is wrong, technical barriers dominate, or the site's strategic direction has changed.
- **A focused connected set is often a better first experiment than many unrelated posts.** Override when audience evidence supports several independent needs. Clusters and internal links do not confer automatic 'topical authority'.
- **Match the content mix to the goal and available proof.** Search-led pieces are a sensible default for an SEO task; sharing-led research or opinion can complement them. Do not impose a universal 60/30/10 mix, a fixed pillar count or a publishing quota.

## Worked decision example
Illustrative only—not observed demand for the current website:
- **Update:** an existing setup guide already addresses a recurring question and has relevant impressions, but its steps are outdated. Refresh the procedure and proof before creating another guide for the same task.
- **Create:** observed template searches and audience requests concern a distinct task no current page serves, and the owner can supply a genuinely usable template. Propose that resource and its supporting explanation.
- **Investigate:** a competitor's new 'alternatives' post looks relevant, but no demand or performance evidence has been checked. Inspect results and audience needs before treating it as a validated target.
- **Defer:** a broad high-volume term is weakly related to the audience, and we have neither distinctive material nor a useful next step for the reader. Revisit if those conditions change.

A compact plan can show candidate, reader task, supporting evidence, existing URL, proposed action, contribution and rationale. These are useful decision aids, not a mandatory table. Handoff selected opportunities to briefing with their evidence and unresolved questions; selecting a topic is not approval to draft it.

## Tools and integrations
Use existing knowledge, research and content records. Connected search and page-reading tools help investigate gaps. Search Console, analytics, keyword data and AI-visibility reports can enrich the decision when available and relevant.

## Useful output
A reasoned recommendation about what to do next, what to update rather than create, and what can wait. Give enough context for the owner to choose, including the reader need, useful contribution and likely next step for the reader. A short recommendation or a small topic map may be more useful than an elaborate calendar.

Detailed assignment and brief approval belong to content-briefing.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read canonical Knowledge or agent-files/00-context/, linked Discoveries or agent-files/01-research/, existing pipeline/published pages and relevant agent-files/04-measurement/ records. Reference those inputs rather than copying them into a new database.

Save the plan in its existing agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/discoveries/ record, or, for production-owned work, agent-files/02-pipeline/backlog.md or the established cluster plan. Keep one canonical plan, with opportunities linked to evidence, existing pages and any later briefs. Update feedback/priorities there and retain meaningful decisions. New raw research belongs in a dated agent-files/01-research/ folder linked from the plan. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; any app recovery copy is an archive, not a second live plan.

skills.desc: Scaffold, draft, revise and prepare assets from an approved brief using existing owner playbooks. Preserve approved text and designer assets.
skills.body:
---
name: "content-production"
description: "Scaffold, draft, revise and prepare assets from an approved brief using existing owner playbooks. Preserve approved text and designer assets."
---

# Content production

## Goal
Create content that does the job agreed in the brief: help the reader understand something, make a decision or accomplish a task, in a voice that fits the site.

## Suggested approach
Begin with the approved brief, what we know about the audience and the owner's feedback. Read the relevant voice and article-format playbooks. An approved direction gives room for writing judgment, not permission to replace the intended angle.

Develop a structure that makes the answer easy to follow, then draft around the reader's needs. Choose the level of detail and format for the material. Use concrete examples and direct explanations rather than filling a target word count.

Research and verify important claims as the draft develops. Bring useful questions back to the owner, especially when their experience or original work would improve the piece. Incorporate what they tell you rather than freezing the draft around the first interpretation.

Use visuals when they clarify something that prose handles poorly. Product screenshots should show real behavior; diagrams and other images should support the explanation. Keep editable sources and useful attribution, captions and alt text. Preserve approved copy and designer assets when making scoped revisions, and ask for missing source material rather than inventing it.

Test runnable examples where appropriate and inspect produced visuals or page previews on desktop and mobile. Read the whole piece for factual accuracy, clarity, useful links and a natural next step. Distinguish what has actually been tested from what remains uncertain.

Share a reviewable result and respond to feedback on the same content item. Editorial review and the owner's readiness approval follow drafting; this skill does not replace those decisions.

## Practical writing methods

### Build the piece around a reader promise
Restate privately what the reader should understand, decide or be able to do at the end. Check the approved brief and relevant voice/format playbooks, then scaffold headings around the reader's questions. Put each section's main point and evidence under its heading before polishing prose. A gap in proof is a research task, not a prompt to write a confident placeholder. Material changes to the approved promise return to briefing.

Read representative approved writing to learn the actual voice: degree of technical detail, use of examples, sentence rhythm and how the author makes recommendations. A founder communication guide is useful for owner-facing notes but is not automatically the public audience's voice. Do not invent first-person experience, customer quotes or familiarity with readers.

### Use the format to do the job
For a tutorial, write from a tested path: prerequisites, action, expected result and verification, with troubleshooting where the reader will need it. Record versions and test limits internally. Clearly distinguish runnable code from intentionally illustrative snippets; never present untested commands as verified.

For a comparison, build the evidence-backed table and decision criteria before the surrounding prose. Give each option comparable treatment, explain which reader it suits and describe real trade-offs. Avoid a generic feature inventory followed by an unsupported universal winner.

For an explainer, introduce the concept in plain language, show a concrete example, then explain distinctions and limits. For a case study, separate observed outcomes from causal interpretation. Use the existing article playbook for the detailed format instead of maintaining another competing template here.

### Draft plainly and concretely
Open with enough context to orient a stranger and deliver the promised answer or route early. Remove generic openings such as 'In today's rapidly evolving landscape'. Define unfamiliar terms before relying on them. Prefer a specific action and example over abstract benefits: instead of 'streamlines review', explain what a person does differently and show it when evidence is available.

Use descriptive headings, paragraphs that develop one idea, ordered lists for sequences and tables for genuinely comparable dimensions. Vary sentence length naturally; brevity should not turn an explanation into unexplained shorthand. Place sources beside the claims they support and figures beside the explanation they clarify. Keep internal research notes out of public copy while retaining uncertainty that materially affects the reader's decision.

### Edit in focused passes
First check the argument and sequence: does every section help deliver the promise? Next check claims, examples, quotations, numbers and source support. Then edit for voice, repetition and sentence-level clarity. Finally inspect the title, description, links, next action and rendered assets. These are separate lenses, not a mandatory number of rewrites. In a scoped correction, apply them to the change and its affected context rather than rewrite the whole page.

Read the headings alone to test the flow. Read the opening and ending together to see whether the promise is fulfilled. Check whether a reader could carry out the procedure or make the choice without guessing at omitted steps. Consolidate owner questions about missing expertise or assets into a useful batch while continuing independent writing work.

## Writing priors to use with judgment
- **Concrete examples usually teach more than additional abstract claims.** Choose examples that genuinely fit; never fabricate customer results or pretend a hypothetical example was observed.
- **Answer early, then earn the detail.** A procedural or decision query usually benefits from a quick answer. A difficult concept may need brief context first; do not force every article into the same opening.
- **Clear beats clever, and complete beats artificially short.** Use the audience's vocabulary and explain necessary technical terms. A slogan is not an explanation.
- **Specific benefits need a mechanism or proof.** Prefer what the reader can do and why it matters over unsupported adjectives such as seamless, revolutionary or best.
- **Length follows the task, not competitors' word counts.** Cut repetition, not the steps or qualifications required for understanding. Do not add FAQ sections, keywords or summaries merely to hit an SEO pattern; follow applicable owner format requirements.
- **Formatting should expose structure, not substitute for reasoning.** Not every paragraph needs bullets or bold text. Owner-approved typography and voice rules take precedence; punctuation bans are style preferences, not evidence of AI authorship.
- **The next action should continue the reader's task.** A useful resource or related guide may fit better than an abrupt sales pitch. Do not invent urgency or force a product mention into every section.

Deliver the draft, supporting assets and a short handoff explaining significant choices and genuinely missing material. Keep the editorial copy separate from that handoff. Do not describe it as publish-ready merely because the prose is polished.

## Tools and integrations
Use the existing content records and relevant playbooks, including the voice guide. Prefer connected search and page retrieval for research, a browser for genuine screenshots and previews, and appropriate image tools for assets. Where generated covers are requested, follow the existing cover playbook and available image-generation integration.

## Useful output
A coherent draft with the examples and assets it needs, ready for a meaningful editorial conversation. Explain significant choices or missing material to the owner without putting internal research notes and diagnostics into the public copy. Keep the draft connected to its brief, evidence and feedback.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read the canonical approved brief and linked research, voice, examples and feedback. Use its owning folder: agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/ for production work or agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/ for app work. Preserve the same content identity.

Save the working draft to the existing draft file (normally draft.md), assets under assets/, and visual-source notes, evidence and revision feedback beside it using established filenames. Keep editable visual sources distinct from exports, linking both in asset notes. New captures belong in raw/ beside their synthesis or in the linked research folder.

Update the same draft as feedback arrives and retain meaningful version/approval history. Website-format exports belong in the publishing target when preparing the authorized handoff, not as a separate independent writing record. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; app recovery copies are marked archives.

Keep internal research notes out of public copy while retaining uncertainty that materially affects the reader's decision.

### Edit in focused passes
First check the argument and sequence: does every section help deliver the promise? Next check claims, examples, quotations, numbers and source support. Then edit for voice, repetition and sentence-level clarity. Finally inspect the title, description, links, next action and rendered assets. These are separate lenses, not a mandatory number of rewrites. In a scoped correction, apply them to the change and its affected context rather than rewrite the whole page.

Read the headings alone to test the flow. Read the opening and ending together to see whether the promise is fulfilled. Check whether a reader could carry out the procedure or make the choice without guessing at omitted steps. Consolidate owner questions about missing expertise or assets into a useful batch while continuing independent writing work.

## Writing priors to use with judgment
- **Concrete examples usually teach more than additional abstract claims.** Choose examples that genuinely fit; never fabricate customer results or pretend a hypothetical example was observed.
- **Answer early, then earn the detail.** A procedural or decision query usually benefits from a quick answer. A difficult concept may need brief context first; do not force every article into the same opening.
- **Clear beats clever, and complete beats artificially short.** Use the audience's vocabulary and explain necessary technical terms. A slogan is not an explanation.
- **Specific benefits need a mechanism or proof.** Prefer what the reader can do and why it matters over unsupported adjectives such as seamless, revolutionary or best.
- **Length follows the task, not competitors' word counts.** Cut repetition, not the steps or qualifications required for understanding. Do not add FAQ sections, keywords or summaries merely to hit an SEO pattern; follow applicable owner format requirements.
- **Formatting should expose structure, not substitute for reasoning.** Not every paragraph needs bullets or bold text. Owner-approved typography and voice rules take precedence; punctuation bans are style preferences, not evidence of AI authorship.
- **The next action should continue the reader's task.** A useful resource or related guide may fit better than an abrupt sales pitch. Do not invent urgency or force a product mention into every section.

Deliver the draft, supporting assets and a short handoff explaining significant choices and genuinely missing material. Keep the editorial copy separate from that handoff. Do not describe it as publish-ready merely because the prose is polished.

## Tools and integrations
Use the existing content records and relevant playbooks, including the voice guide. Prefer connected search and page retrieval for research, a browser for genuine screenshots and previews, and appropriate image tools for assets. Where generated covers are requested, follow the existing cover playbook and available image-generation integration.

## Useful output
A coherent draft with the examples and assets it needs, ready for a meaningful editorial conversation. Explain significant choices or missing material to the owner without putting internal research notes and diagnostics into the public copy. Keep the draft connected to its brief, evidence and feedback.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read the canonical approved brief and linked research, voice, examples and feedback. Use its owning folder: agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/ for production work or agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/ for app work. Preserve the same content identity.

Save the working draft to the existing draft file (normally draft.md), assets under assets/, and visual-source notes, evidence and revision feedback beside it using established filenames. Keep editable visual sources distinct from exports, linking both in asset notes. New captures belong in raw/ beside their synthesis or in the linked research folder.

Update the same draft as feedback arrives and retain meaningful version/approval history. Website-format exports belong in the publishing target when preparing the authorized handoff, not as a separate independent writing record. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; app recovery copies are marked archives.

skills.name: content-refresh
skills.desc: Diagnose outdated or declining content and prepare or execute a scoped refresh through briefing, production and review, without implicit republishing permission.
skills.body:
---
name: "content-refresh"
description: "Diagnose outdated or declining content and prepare or execute a scoped refresh through briefing, production and review, without implicit republishing permission."
---

# Content refresh

## Goal
Keep existing content useful as the website, audience and surrounding information change. Work out whether a page needs attention and what kind of improvement would matter, rather than rewriting it simply because it is old.

## Suggested approach
Read the existing page, its intended purpose, previous feedback and any relevant history. Understand why a refresh is being considered: outdated facts, a reader problem, changed search intent, broken assets or a performance concern. Ask the owner about changes the public page may not yet reflect.

Investigate the affected material and compare it with current sources and audience needs. When performance data is available, compare like periods and consider seasonality, incomplete data, technical issues and measurement changes before concluding the content has deteriorated. A factual update can still be worthwhile without analytics; it should not be described as a response to measured decline without evidence.

Recommend the appropriate level of work. That may be leaving the page alone, correcting a detail, improving an explanation, adding new proof or revisiting the angle. Consider consolidation only when it genuinely helps readers, not just because two pages share keywords.

Explain the important changes to the owner and clarify questions that affect direction. Substantial changes should go through the brief discussion and approval; a specifically requested small correction should not turn into an unrelated rewrite.

Use the production and editorial-review skills to carry out the agreed work. Preserve useful approved material and the page's history. Check affected examples, links and visuals, and keep publication decisions under the current publishing workflow. URL moves, deletions and redirects need their own authorization.

After publication, suggest an appropriate way to learn whether the change helped. Choose a useful observation period and outcome for the page rather than promising a recovery or inventing a schedule.

## Practical diagnosis and refresh format

### Establish what changed
Begin with the page's purpose, original publication and meaningful update dates, current state and the reason for review. For a factual correction, verify the affected material directly; analytics is optional. For reported performance decline, inspect comparable complete periods and, where useful, year-over-year context. Use the same property, URL grouping, search type, country/device and filters. Consider traffic volume and normal variability before choosing a window; there is no universal number of days that establishes decay.

Read clicks, impressions, CTR and position together, plus qualified outcomes where tracking is available. Lower impressions may reflect lower demand or lost visibility. Stable impressions with lower clicks may reflect changed result presentation, query mix or CTR. Lower conversions with stable traffic may involve audience mix, tracking or the visitor journey. These are hypotheses, not diagnoses. Check query/page segments, technical state and recent site changes before blaming the copy.

### Compare the page with today's task
Revisit relevant current results and audience questions. Look for a changed reader task, outdated procedure, missing example, broken asset or unsupported claim. Compare the page's promise with what it actually delivers. Use competitor pages to identify questions worth examining, not to justify copying everything they added. Preserve useful original material and recognize where the page already answers the question well.

### Propose the smallest useful intervention
A refresh note can contain: current URL and purpose; evidence/reason; recommended change; sections to keep; sections/assets to update; proof needed; approval scope; and how to judge the result. Use a short note for a small fix and a fuller brief when the angle changes.

Useful options include leaving the page unchanged, repairing a technical problem, correcting facts, improving an example or procedure, adjusting a misleading title, or substantially rebriefing the piece. Recommend consolidation only after examining distinct intents, links and the consequences for each URL. Do not change dates just to simulate freshness, expand length without a reader need, or rename URLs for cosmetic SEO.

### Recheck and learn
After approved work, use production and review rather than duplicate their methods. Check that the fix solves the original issue and has not broken other content. Record the actual publication date separately from draft completion. Compare later results with the baseline after a suitable observation period, noting seasonality, other releases and instrumentation changes. Suggest an observation plan without creating a schedule unless requested. A before/after improvement is not by itself proof of causation.

## Refresh priors and examples
- **Accuracy problems deserve repair even without a traffic decline.** An outdated command is a concrete defect. Correct and test it within the authorized scope rather than waiting for analytics.
- **Technical and measurement failures come before speculative rewrites.** If the page was accidentally noindex or tracking stopped, investigate that first. More paragraphs will not fix those problems.
- **A narrow evidence-backed improvement is often preferable to replacing the whole article.** Override when the reader's task or approved direction has genuinely changed and a new brief is approved.
- **Age alone is weak evidence of a problem.** A stable reference may need no change; a recent pricing comparison may already be outdated.
- **Preserve what is working, but do not treat past rankings as proof of current quality.** Keep useful examples and established URLs by default while evaluating present needs.

Illustrative decisions: fix a broken tutorial step when the interface changes; investigate seasonal demand before rewriting a guide whose impressions declined; propose a new brief when the query now calls for a different type of resource. These examples are starting reasoning patterns, not findings about the current website.

## Tools and integrations
Use existing content and history, connected search and webpage retrieval, and the production/review tools needed for the change. Search Console or the site's analytics can help investigate performance where relevant; ask for access or exports when that evidence is needed.

## Useful output
An explanation of whether to refresh the page and why, followed by the agreed improvement when authorized. Keep enough history to understand what changed and to compare later results. Match the depth of reporting to the size of the change.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Start with the original identity/publication record. Production content uses agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/ and live records in agent-files/03-published/. App content stays in agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/; Published is a view of the same identity. Read linked performance from agent-files/04-measurement/ and existing research notes.

Save rationale, scope and changes beside the original brief/draft in its existing refresh note, or refresh.md. Keep dated performance exports and source/filter details in the established measurement location or agent-files/04-measurement/<slug>/<dated-run>/raw/. Link baseline and later measurements to the refresh note. Save new public research and raw evidence under a dated agent-files/01-research/ folder.

Update the original draft through production/review rather than creating another article. After verified publication update the original live record, preserving its history. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions. App-owned records remain authoritative; recovery snapshots are explicitly archived copies.

skills.name: editorial-seo-review
skills.desc: Check facts, editorial quality, positioning, SEO, links, attribution, visuals and conversion before the owner's publish-readiness decision.
skills.body:
---
name: "editorial-seo-review"
description: "Check facts, editorial quality, positioning, SEO, links, attribution, visuals and conversion before the owner's publish-readiness decision."
---

# Editorial and SEO review

## Goal
Help the owner publish something accurate, useful and well presented. Review from the reader's perspective as well as the site's goals, finding meaningful problems rather than performing checklist theatre.

## Suggested approach
Read the current draft, approved brief and relevant owner feedback. Understand what the piece is trying to do and the voice it should use. Use the existing pre-publish quality playbook as supporting guidance, applying its checks to the actual page and publishing target.

Assess whether the piece answers its intended question, explains important ideas clearly and contributes something useful. Look for unsupported claims, unfair comparisons, confusing structure or distracting repetition. Check consequential facts against relevant evidence and discuss questions that the owner is better placed to answer.

Examine the reader's practical experience: links, figures, captions, examples, mobile layout and the next action the page offers. Verify metadata and relevant SEO details in the actual publishing format. A rendered preview shows things the Markdown alone cannot; distinguish preview findings from checks that need the live page.

Prioritize issues that affect trust, usefulness or publication. Make authorized corrections without rewriting unrelated approved material. Keep technical detail available for fixing problems, but present the owner with the decisions and changes that matter.

Use judgment about what applies. An old checklist's reference to a different CMS is not a reason to duplicate records. Structured data should reflect the visible page and current search guidance, not a promise of special search placement. If a necessary check cannot be performed, explain what remains unverified.

The existing factual, editorial, positioning, technical SEO, link, attribution and conversion checks still apply before readiness. The owner approves the reviewed version before it moves to Ready to publish; material changes need renewed approval.

## Practical review passes
Start with the actual version under review, not an earlier approved screenshot or a plan. Use the owner checklist and publishing specification for detailed requirements. The following lenses help prioritize the work without creating another competing checklist.

### Promise, structure and voice
Compare the title, opening, main answer and next action with the approved brief. Read headings alone, then read the whole piece. Look for missing prerequisites, repeated sections, unexplained terms and conclusions that do not follow from the body. For tutorials, can the reader complete the task? For comparisons, are the criteria consistent and recommendations tied to reader needs? For explanations, does the example actually clarify the idea? Distinguish a defect from your stylistic preference before changing approved copy.

### Claims and proof
Trace consequential facts to the cited material, not merely to a source that mentions the topic. Check the exact number, denominator, date, product version, plan and limitations where relevant. Confirm that a citation supports the claim's strength; a vendor assertion is not an independent test. Verify quotations and ensure hypotheticals are recognizable. An absent feature in documentation does not prove a product cannot do it.

Inspect superlatives and causal language especially carefully. 'Fastest', 'secure' and 'increased revenue' need the relevant comparison, threat model or measurement. Qualify, substantiate or remove unsupported claims rather than hide them behind fluent wording. Keep the evidence trail internal, but leave decision-relevant limitations visible to readers.

### Reader experience and publishing format
Follow important links to their intended destinations, not just a successful status code. Check links to planned pages are not presented as live. Inspect code and procedural examples against their test evidence; retest changed steps when feasible. Open every asset, including the last figure, and inspect the rendered page on desktop and mobile for legibility, crop, overflow, captions and placement.

Verify title/description, canonical, robots directives and relevant structured data in the actual output where available. Check that social metadata uses the intended cover, and that citations and attribution survive formatting. A preview can intentionally be noindex; distinguish that from an accidental production directive. Record live-only checks as pending rather than claiming preview evidence proves live indexing.

### Resolve and hand off
Correct authorized defects and recheck affected behavior. Group remaining issues by what prevents publication, what needs an owner decision and what is optional. For each substantial issue, provide the location, evidence and a concrete fix. Example: 'The table says all plans include export, but the cited pricing page limits it to a paid tier. Correct the row and recheck the paragraph that repeats it.'

The owner-facing summary should say what changed, what still matters and what decision is requested. Detailed checks remain in internal review notes. A useful handoff can be: recommendation, important fixes, unresolved blockers and the reviewed-version link. No rigid score is needed. Owner approval is still required for Ready to publish; the review cannot grant it.

## Review priors
Trust and usability failures usually matter more than cosmetic SEO conventions. Review important claims and actual behavior before polishing wording. A failed source lookup is unknown, not permission to guess; a missing test is unverified, not passed. Preserve strong approved passages rather than rewrite for novelty. Fixed word counts, keyword density and AI-detector scores are not reliable quality verdicts. A technically valid page can still be unhelpful, and excellent prose can still contain publication blockers.

## Tools and integrations
Read the draft, evidence, voice guide and existing pre-publish playbook. Use connected page retrieval for verification, HTTP checks for links and headers, and the site's build/preview tools and browser for rendered inspection. Choose tools to answer actual review questions rather than connecting every possible service.

## Useful output
A concise editorial assessment, important corrections and any decisions needed from the owner, supported by internal review notes. Make clear what was checked and what still needs attention. The result should make review easier, not make the owner interpret an audit database.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read draft, brief, feedback, assets and evidence from the owning folder: agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/ or agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/. Publishing spec and voice/context remain in their canonical Knowledge or agent-files/00-context/ records.

Save internal findings to the existing review note beside the draft, or review.md for a first review. Keep screenshots and link/build verification evidence in a dated review-evidence/ subfolder, linked to the reviewed version and preview/live URL. Attach the owner-facing summary and feedback to the same content record/request, not a second draft or diagnostic app view.

Link original source evidence instead of duplicating research. Preserve earlier reviews for materially different versions. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; mark app recovery copies as archives.

skills.name: learn-business-context
skills.desc: Learn the purpose, audience and context of a business or website through public research, useful private materials and conversation with its owner. Use for onboarding or updating that understanding.
skills.body:
---
name: "learn-business-context"
description: "Learn the purpose, audience and context of a business or website through public research, useful private materials and conversation with its owner. Use for onboarding or updating that understanding."
---

# Learn business context

## Goal
Understand the website and the person behind it well enough to make useful content recommendations. Approach this like a freelancer getting to know a new client: do your homework, form an initial picture, and improve it through conversation.

The site might represent a business, an artist, a community or a hobby. Adapt what you investigate and ask to its purpose rather than forcing every owner into a business framework.

## Suggested approach

### Start with what is already known
Look through the conversation and existing notes. Identify the website from that information; if needed, ask for the website and a little essential context together. For an ongoing relationship, build on what you have already learned rather than starting the interview again.

Work in batches that respect the user's time. Explain what you will research and what they can expect next, then complete a useful research pass before returning with your initial picture and a short batch of related questions. Avoid repeatedly asking one question, spending several minutes researching, and coming back for another. This is an asynchronous-friendly conversation, not a promise of background execution.

### Research the public picture
Explore the website and relevant public information. The homepage, about page, products or services, published work, articles, reviews and social presence can reveal what the owner does, whom they reach and how they present themselves.

Do enough light market and competitor research to understand the surrounding landscape. Consider not only similar businesses or sites, but other ways the audience meets the same need. This is orientation, not an exhaustive competitive study.

Build an initial interpretation of the site's purpose, audience, offer or subject matter, positioning and voice. Keep useful links and notes so important conclusions can be revisited. Be clear where you are interpreting rather than repeating something the owner has confirmed.

### Invite additional context
Ask whether the user has useful material in Notion, Google Drive or elsewhere that they would like to connect or share. Examples include research, company information, customer conversations, strategy notes or previous content plans. If they do, use it to deepen or challenge the public picture. Public research can still be useful without private documents.

### Discuss and refine your understanding
Share a concise view of what you think you have learned, then group the questions that would most improve the next piece of work into a small, answerable batch. Include the invitation to share private material when it fits, rather than creating another interruption just for that. Explain what their answers will help you do next. Keep this conversational, not a long questionnaire or a step-by-step interview.

Let the user's answers change your interpretation and guide further investigation. We do not need a complete understanding on day one: address what matters now and learn the rest through ongoing work.

Useful areas to explore may include:
- What the business or website exists to do, and what success looks like to its owner.
- Who it serves, what those people want, and how they describe their needs.
- Its products, services or subject matter, and its business model where relevant.
- The alternatives its audience considers and what makes this site worth choosing or returning to.
- Questions, objections or misunderstandings the content should address.
- Experience, examples or other proof the owner can contribute.
- The voice they want and what they hope a visitor will do next.

Choose the areas that matter to this project. An artist may care about commissions or showing their work; a hobby site may care about sharing knowledge or building a community. Do not invent commercial goals where there are none.

### Keep the understanding useful

skills.name: market-competitor-research
skills.desc: Research competitors' SEO and content strategies: blog topics, intent, ranking keywords and top pages where data is available. Identify search competitors and opportunities for useful content.
skills.body:
---
name: "market-competitor-research"
description: "Research competitors' SEO and content strategies: blog topics, intent, ranking keywords and top pages where data is available. Identify search competitors and opportunities for useful content."
---

# Market and competitor research

## Goal
Understand how competitors use content to attract the audience we care about, what appears to work for them, and where our website can make a useful contribution. This is primarily SEO and content research, not a general product-feature comparison. Market context helps interpret the content strategy, but should not displace analysis of published pages.

## Suggested approach
Start with existing business context, research and the decision this work should support. Identify direct competitors and sites competing for the same search attention, including publishers and communities without competing products. Explain the research plan, investigate in a useful batch, then return with findings and a small group of questions where owner input would help.

Prioritize blogs and other search-oriented content: guides, tutorials, comparison and alternatives pages, templates, tools and topic hubs. Explore blog indexes, categories, sitemaps and representative articles. Notice recurring topics, intended readers, questions, formats, depth, publication/update patterns, internal links and calls to action. Visible dates and listings can be incomplete; explain sample coverage.

Read the posts themselves to understand what the competitor seems to be trying to achieve. Beginner guides may suggest category education; alternatives pages may target people considering a switch; templates may attract people ready to implement. These are interpretations of editorial intent, not proof of success. Product or pricing pages help explain how content connects to the offer, rather than becoming the main subject of research.

If Ahrefs, Semrush or a comparable provider is available, investigate ranking keywords and top-performing organic pages. Keep keywords, ranking URLs, positions, country/database, observation date and available volume/traffic estimates connected. Define 'top-performing', for example by estimated organic traffic, rather than implying knowledge of conversions or revenue. Use comparable filters across sites and retain provider limitations.

Without those tools, public posts still reveal targeting, topic clusters, formats and likely visitor journeys. Do not call sampled pages top performers merely because they are prominent or recent. Distinguish provider estimates or observed rankings from inferred keyword targets. Publishing on a topic does not by itself validate demand for our own page.

Compare their approach with our existing content and expertise. Look for relevant coverage gaps, weak or outdated answers, useful formats and questions we can answer with stronger examples or proof. Recommend what to investigate, improve or create, not copying their calendar wholesale. Refine findings through owner feedback without requiring every question answered on day one.

## Tools and integrations
Prefer available search and page-reading tools such as Composio web search and Context.dev. Use discovery/configuration capabilities when available to find suitable search, scraping or SEO data tools and enable them within authorized scope. Reuse ready connections; request authentication only where needed. Ahrefs and Semrush are options, not claims of connected access. Supplied exports can also help when their source, scope and date are known.

Browser or direct HTTP can fill retrieval gaps. General web search supports discovery but is not a localized Google ranking capture unless it actually provides that evidence. Ask about private research the owner is willing to share when it would improve interpretation.

## Useful output
An explanation of competitors' SEO and content strategies, supported by representative posts and available keyword/top-page data. Show the audiences and intents they seem to target, what is demonstrably performing versus inferred, and implications for our next decisions. Profiles, page inventories, topic maps or comparison tables should serve that explanation.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read canonical context from agent-files/00-context/ and existing research from agent-files/01-research/. For app-owned work, follow linked records in agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/knowledge/, inputs/ and discoveries/. Inputs include competitor domains, the research question, prior findings and available exports.

Reuse the canonical competitor research folder, currently agent-files/01-research/competitor-map/, with dated investigation subfolders. Save original page captures and provider responses/exports in raw/ beside the analysis, retaining URL, retrieval date, locale, filters and units. A page inventory can connect each domain, URL, topic, inferred intent and metrics without forcing a fixed report template. Preserve earlier snapshots for future comparisons.

Save the synthesis in the existing app Discovery when it owns the work; otherwise keep it in the durable research folder. Link the synthesis to raw evidence and relevant Knowledge. Update existing competitor notes instead of creating duplicate active profiles. Any durable recovery copy of app-owned work is labeled an archive, not a second editable record. Update agent-files/INDEX.md so planning and briefing can find the result.

## Scope
The focus is competitors' search and content activity. Detailed product trials, backlink campaigns, article writing and monitoring are separate work when requested.
